subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: Explain the uses of computers in nursing practice, nursing education, nursing research and nursing administration.
answer_html:
Introduction Computers are now part of every area of health care. In hospitals they record patient data, order medicines and display test results; in colleges they support teaching and online learning; in research they store and analyse data. A nurse who can use computers confidently gives safer, faster and better-documented care.

A. Uses in nursing practice (patient care)

  1. Electronic documentation – admission assessment, vital signs, nursing notes, care plans and discharge summaries recorded in the electronic health record
  2. Medication management – electronic medication administration record (eMAR), barcode scanning, alerts for allergies and drug interactions, dose calculators
  3. Patient monitoring – bedside monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps linked to computers; early warning scores and alarms
  4. Orders and results – receiving doctors' orders electronically; viewing laboratory, X-ray and other reports quickly
  5. Clinical decision support – reminders, care protocols and standard nursing care plans
  6. Communication – between wards, departments and the health team; handover reports
  7. Telenursing and telemedicine – follow-up and teaching of patients at home
  8. Patient education – videos, presentations and mobile apps for teaching patients

B. Uses in nursing education

  1. Computer-assisted instruction (CAI) – tutorials, drills, quizzes and simulations
  2. E-learning and online classes – learning management systems (e.g. Moodle, Google Classroom), video lectures, webinars, MOOCs (e.g. SWAYAM)
  3. Multimedia presentations – PowerPoint, animations and videos of procedures
  4. Simulation – high-fidelity manikins and virtual patients controlled by computers
  5. Online examinations, assignment submission, plagiarism checking and record of attendance and marks
  6. Access to e-books, e-journals and digital libraries
  7. Communication between teachers and students – e-mail, discussion forums, messaging groups

C. Uses in nursing research

  1. Literature search in databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, Shodhganga)
  2. Data collection – online questionnaires (e.g. Google Forms), mobile data-collection apps
  3. Data entry, storage and management in spreadsheets and databases
  4. Statistical analysis – SPSS, Excel, R, Epi Info
  5. Presentation of results – tables, graphs and charts; writing reports and theses with word processors
  6. Reference management – Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote
  7. Publication and sharing of research online

D. Uses in nursing administration

  1. Staffing and scheduling – duty rosters, leave records, workload and patient-acuity calculations
  2. Personnel records – qualifications, training, performance appraisal
  3. Inventory and supplies – stock of drugs, linen and equipment; indenting and purchase
  4. Budgeting and cost analysis
  5. Quality assurance – incident reports, infection-control data, audits, quality indicators (bed occupancy, falls, pressure ulcers)
  6. Hospital information system – admission, discharge, billing, bed management
  7. Communication – circulars, notices, meetings by video conference

E. Advantages and limitations

  • Advantages – speed, accuracy, legible and complete records, easy retrieval, saves time and paper, better communication and decision making
  • Limitations – cost of equipment and training, need for constant power and internet, risk of data loss, hacking and breach of confidentiality, system failure (downtime), less face-to-face time with patients if not used wisely

F. Examples from Indian health care

  • e-Hospital and similar hospital management systems in many government hospitals – registration, OPD, admission, laboratory and pharmacy modules
  • Online Registration System (ORS) for appointments in large public hospitals
  • eSanjeevani – the national telemedicine service for teleconsultation from health and wellness centres and homes
  • Programme portals – Nikshay (tuberculosis patients), U-WIN (routine immunisation), RCH portal (mothers and children), HMIS portal (monthly facility reports), used by nurses and ANMs
  • Digital records linked to the ABHA health ID under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission

G. Competencies a nurse needs

  • Basic computer skills – typing, file management, e-mail, word processing and spreadsheets
  • Information literacy – finding, evaluating and using reliable information
  • Use of clinical systems – documentation, eMAR, order entry, monitoring devices
  • Data protection – passwords, logging out, confidentiality, safe use of mobile phones
  • Problem reporting – recognising system errors and following downtime procedures
  • Willingness to learn new technology through in-service education

H. Emerging trends

  • Artificial intelligence for early warning of deterioration and image reading
  • Robots for medicine dispensing and telepresence
  • Wearable devices and smart beds that monitor patients continuously
  • Mobile apps for patient teaching and remote follow-up

Conclusion Computers support nursing practice through documentation, medication safety, monitoring and communication; nursing education through e-learning and simulation; research through literature search, data analysis and reporting; and administration through staffing, inventory, budgeting and quality control, provided they are used safely and with attention to confidentiality.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: Describe MS Word, MS Excel and MS PowerPoint and their uses in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Microsoft Office is a package of application software. Its three most commonly used programs – Word (word processing), Excel (spreadsheets) and PowerPoint (presentations) – are used every day by nurses, nursing students and teachers. Similar free programs include LibreOffice and Google Docs, Sheets and Slides.

A. MS Word (word processor)

1. Meaning – a program for creating, editing, formatting, saving and printing documents

2. Main features

  • Typing and editing text; cut, copy and paste; undo
  • Formatting – font type, size, bold, italic, underline, colour; alignment, line spacing, bullets and numbering
  • Tables, pictures, shapes and charts
  • Spell check and grammar check, word count, find and replace
  • Headers, footers, page numbers, margins, page orientation
  • Templates, styles, table of contents, footnotes and references
  • Mail merge – the same letter to many people
  • Track changes and comments for reviewing
  • Saving as .docx or PDF; printing

3. Uses in nursing

  • Writing nursing care plans, case studies, assignments and project reports
  • Preparing letters, circulars, notices, reports and minutes of meetings
  • Procedure manuals, policies and standard forms
  • Health education leaflets and handouts
  • Theses and research reports with tables and references

B. MS Excel (spreadsheet)

1. Meaning – a program that arranges data in rows and columns (cells) and performs calculations and charts

2. Main features

  • Worksheets and workbooks; cells identified by column letter and row number (e.g. B5)
  • Formulas beginning with "=" – e.g. =SUM(B2:B10), =AVERAGE(), =MAX(), =MIN(), =COUNT(), =IF()
  • Sorting and filtering data; conditional formatting (e.g. highlighting high values)
  • Charts – bar, column, line, pie, scatter
  • Pivot tables for summarising data; basic statistics (Analysis ToolPak)

3. Uses in nursing

  • Duty rosters and leave records
  • Inventory of drugs, linen and equipment; stock registers
  • Calculation of intake–output, drug doses and IV drip rates
  • Ward statistics – bed occupancy, admissions, discharges, infection rates
  • Student attendance and marks
  • Research data entry and simple analysis with graphs

C. MS PowerPoint (presentation software)

1. Meaning – a program for creating slide presentations with text, pictures, charts, audio and video

2. Main features

  • Slides with layouts and themes (designs)
  • Inserting pictures, charts, tables, SmartArt, audio and video
  • Transitions between slides and animations of objects
  • Slide show mode, presenter view, speaker notes
  • Handouts and printing; saving as PDF or video

3. Uses in nursing

  • Classroom teaching, seminars, case presentations, journal clubs
  • Health education for patients and the community
  • Presenting research findings at conferences
  • Orientation and in-service education of staff

4. Guidelines for a good presentation

  • One idea per slide; about 5–6 lines, short phrases; large readable fonts (24 point or more)
  • Simple, consistent design; contrasting colours; relevant pictures
  • Limited animation; practise timing; cite sources

D. Common keyboard shortcuts and file management

  • Ctrl + C copy, Ctrl + X cut, Ctrl + V paste, Ctrl + Z undo, Ctrl + S save, Ctrl + P print, Ctrl + F find, Ctrl + B / I / U bold, italic, underline
  • Save files with clear names in organised folders (e.g. "Ward5_Roster_Nov2026"); save frequently and keep backups
  • Cloud storage (OneDrive, Google Drive) allows access from any device and shared editing

E. Example – an intake–output sheet in Excel

  • Column A: time; column B: oral intake; column C: IV intake; column D: urine; column E: other output
  • Cell B26 =SUM(B2:B25) gives total oral intake; cell F27 =(B26+C26)-(D26+E26) gives the fluid balance
  • A line chart shows the hourly urine output trend

F. Precautions

  • Do not store identifiable patient data on personal computers or pen drives; de-identify data used for assignments and research
  • Password-protect files containing confidential information
  • Check spelling and calculations before printing or sending

G. Free alternatives and online collaboration

  • LibreOffice (free desktop suite) and Google Docs, Sheets and Slides (online)
  • Several people can edit the same file at once, add comments and see the version history – useful for group assignments and ward rosters
  • Use sharing settings carefully – share only with the people who need access

H. Simple steps – inserting a chart in Excel

  1. Select the data (e.g. months and number of admissions)
  2. Click Insert → Chart and choose the chart type (column or line)
  3. Add a title and axis labels; format colours
  4. Copy the chart into a Word report or PowerPoint slide

Conclusion MS Word is used to prepare and format documents such as care plans and reports, MS Excel to organise data and perform calculations and charts for rosters, inventories and statistics, and MS PowerPoint to create slide presentations for teaching, health education and research, making all three essential tools for nurses.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: Explain the basic components of a computer.
answer_html:
Introduction A computer is an electronic machine that accepts data (input), processes it according to instructions, stores it, and gives results (output). It has two main parts – hardware and software.

1. Hardware – the physical parts that can be seen and touched

a. Input devices – used to enter data and instructions

  • Keyboard, mouse, touch screen, scanner, barcode reader, microphone, webcam, biometric (fingerprint) reader

b. Central processing unit (CPU) – the "brain" of the computer

  • Arithmetic logic unit (ALU) – performs calculations and comparisons
  • Control unit (CU) – directs and coordinates all operations
  • Registers – small, fast storage within the CPU

c. Memory

  • Primary memory – RAM (random access memory – temporary, lost when power is off) and ROM (read-only memory – permanent start-up instructions)
  • Secondary storage – hard disk, solid-state drive (SSD), pen drive, memory card, CD/DVD, cloud storage – store data permanently

d. Output devices – display or produce the results

  • Monitor, printer, speakers, projector

e. Other – motherboard, power supply, network card, modem/router for internet

2. Software – the set of programs (instructions) that tell the hardware what to do

  • System software – the operating system (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android) that manages the computer; utility programs (antivirus, backup)
  • Application software – programs for specific tasks – MS Office, web browsers, hospital information system, statistical packages, e-learning apps

3. Other elements

  • Data – raw facts entered into the computer
  • Users (peopleware) – those who operate the computer
  • Network – connection of computers to share data (LAN, internet)

Use in nursing – knowing the basic parts helps nurses use computers, barcode scanners and printers correctly, store data safely and report problems.

4. Types of computers

  • Supercomputers and mainframes – very large, used for research and national databases
  • Servers – store and share data on a network (e.g. the hospital information system server)
  • Personal computers – desktop, laptop, tablet and smartphone
  • Embedded computers – inside medical devices such as monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps

5. Units of memory – bit (0 or 1) → byte (8 bits) → kilobyte (KB) → megabyte (MB) → gigabyte (GB) → terabyte (TB), each about 1,024 times the previous unit

Conclusion A computer consists of hardware – input devices, CPU, memory and storage, and output devices – and software – system and application programs – which work together to accept, process, store and present data.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: Explain the uses of the internet in nursing. Add a note on safe use.
answer_html:
Introduction The internet is a worldwide network of connected computers that allows people to share information and communicate. For nurses it is a powerful tool for learning, practice and communication.

1. Uses in nursing

  • Access to information – e-books, e-journals, guidelines (WHO, ICMR, MoHFW), drug information, nursing websites
  • Literature search – databases such as PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar
  • E-learning – online courses, webinars, video demonstrations, continuing nursing education (CNE)
  • Communication – e-mail, video conferencing, messaging, professional forums and networks
  • Telehealth and telenursing – teleconsultation, remote monitoring, follow-up of patients
  • Health education – sharing reliable information with patients and communities
  • Online services – registration and renewal with nursing councils, examination results, job applications, online purchase of supplies
  • Research – online surveys, data sharing, publishing papers

2. Limitations

  • Unreliable or false information (misinformation) on many websites
  • Information overload; distraction
  • Risk of viruses, phishing and hacking; privacy problems
  • Need for internet connection and devices (digital divide)

3. Safe use of the internet

  • Use reliable sources – government, WHO, professional bodies, peer-reviewed journals; check the author, date and evidence
  • Use strong passwords, change them regularly and never share them; use two-step verification
  • Do not open suspicious e-mails, links or attachments (phishing)
  • Keep antivirus software and updates current; use secure (https) websites
  • Log out of shared computers; do not save passwords on public computers
  • Never share patient information or photographs on social media or unsecured messaging
  • Respect copyright – cite sources and do not plagiarise

4. Common internet terms

  • World Wide Web (WWW) – the collection of web pages linked on the internet
  • Web browser – a program to view web pages (Chrome, Firefox, Edge)
  • Search engine – a website for finding information (e.g. Google)
  • URL – the address of a web page (e.g. https://www.who.int)
  • E-mail – electronic messages with attachments
  • Wi-Fi, LAN and WAN – wireless, local and wide area networks connecting computers
  • Cloud – storage and services provided over the internet

Conclusion The internet helps nurses find information, learn, communicate, practise telehealth and conduct research, but it must be used safely, with reliable sources, strong passwords, protection from phishing and strict protection of patient confidentiality.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: Explain the steps of a literature search using electronic databases.
answer_html:
Introduction A literature search is a systematic search for published information on a topic. It is the first step in research and in evidence-based practice. Electronic databases make searching fast, but a planned strategy is needed to find the right articles.

1. Steps of a literature search

  1. Define the question or topic – use the PICO format (Patient/Problem, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome), e.g. "In post-operative patients (P), does incentive spirometry (I) compared with deep breathing alone (C) reduce pneumonia (O)?"
  2. Identify keywords and synonyms – e.g. "pressure ulcer", "bed sore", "decubitus ulcer"; use controlled vocabulary such as MeSH terms in PubMed
  3. Select databases suitable for the topic
  4. Build the search using:
    • Boolean operators – AND (narrows: pressure ulcer AND prevention), OR (widens: bed sore OR pressure ulcer), NOT (excludes)
    • Phrase searching with quotation marks – "hand hygiene"
    • Truncation – nurs* finds nurse, nurses, nursing
  5. Apply filters – years, language, age group, type of study (randomised trial, systematic review), free full text
  6. Screen titles and abstracts; select relevant articles; obtain full texts
  7. Critically evaluate the quality of each study
  8. Record the search (databases, terms, dates) and manage references with tools such as Zotero, Mendeley or EndNote

2. Common databases and sources

  • PubMed/MEDLINE – free biomedical database of the US National Library of Medicine
  • CINAHL – nursing and allied health literature
  • Cochrane Library – systematic reviews
  • Embase, Scopus, Web of Science – large multidisciplinary databases
  • Google Scholar – free, broad search
  • Indian sources – Shodhganga (Indian theses, INFLIBNET), IndMED (Indian biomedical journals), ERMED consortium

3. Tips

  • Prefer recent, peer-reviewed and high-level evidence
  • Avoid relying only on websites and blogs
  • Keep a log of searches so they can be repeated

4. Evaluating sources – the CRAAP test

  • Currency – is the information recent?
  • Relevance – does it answer the question?
  • Authority – who is the author or publisher?
  • Accuracy – is it supported by evidence and peer reviewed?
  • Purpose – is it written to inform, or to sell or persuade?

Conclusion A literature search involves defining the question (PICO), choosing keywords and databases, combining terms with Boolean operators, applying filters, screening and evaluating articles and recording references, using sources such as PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane and Shodhganga.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: Explain the statistical packages used in nursing research.
answer_html:
Introduction Statistical packages are computer programs used to enter, manage, analyse and present research data. They save time, reduce calculation errors and allow complex analysis that would be very difficult by hand.

1. Common statistical packages

  • SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences) – widely used in nursing research; menu-driven; descriptive statistics, t-test, chi-square, correlation, ANOVA, regression; tables and charts
  • Microsoft Excel – spreadsheets with formulas, charts and the Analysis ToolPak for basic statistics; good for data entry and simple analysis
  • R – free, open-source software with powerful statistics and graphics; uses commands (RStudio interface)
  • Epi Info – free software from the CDC for epidemiological data – questionnaires, data entry, analysis and maps
  • STATA, SAS – advanced packages used in large health surveys
  • Others – GraphPad Prism, EpiData, free menu-based tools such as JASP and jamovi

2. Uses in nursing research

  • Data entry and coding, checking for errors and missing values
  • Descriptive statistics – frequency, percentage, mean, median, mode, standard deviation
  • Inferential statistics – testing hypotheses (t-test, chi-square, ANOVA, correlation, regression)
  • Presentation – tables, bar charts, pie charts, histograms
  • Analysis of pre-test and post-test scores in intervention studies

3. Steps in using a package

  1. Plan the analysis according to the objectives
  2. Create the variables (name, type, labels, codes)
  3. Enter and clean the data
  4. Choose and run the correct statistical test
  5. Interpret the output (p-value, confidence interval)
  6. Present results in tables and graphs

4. Precautions – the package only calculates; the researcher must choose the correct test and interpret results correctly; keep data backed up and confidential

5. Examples in nursing research

  • Comparing students' knowledge scores before and after a teaching programme – paired t-test in SPSS or Excel
  • Testing the association between hand-hygiene training and compliance – chi-square test
  • Showing the percentage of patients with different pain scores – bar or pie chart

6. Choosing a package – depends on the cost, the researcher's skill, the size of the data and the tests needed; many institutions hold SPSS licences, while R, jamovi and Epi Info are free alternatives.

Conclusion Statistical packages such as SPSS, Excel, R and Epi Info help nurses enter, analyse and present research data accurately and quickly, but correct choice of tests and interpretation remain the researcher's responsibility.

question: Differentiate between hardware and software.
answer_html:
Hardware Software
Physical parts of a computer that can be seen and touched Programs and instructions that tell the hardware what to do
Examples – keyboard, mouse, monitor, CPU, printer, hard disk Examples – Windows, MS Office, web browser, hospital information system
Can be damaged physically; wears out Can be affected by viruses or bugs; does not wear out
Cannot work without software Needs hardware to run
Replaced when faulty Updated or reinstalled

Firmware – software permanently stored in a hardware chip (e.g. start-up instructions in ROM, programs inside infusion pumps).

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: State the functions of an operating system.
answer_html:
An operating system (OS) is system software that manages the computer and acts as a link between the user, the application programs and the hardware (e.g. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android).

Functions

  1. Starts (boots) the computer and manages its resources
  2. File management – creating, saving, organising, copying and deleting files and folders
  3. Memory and processor management – runs several programs at the same time
  4. Device management – controls the keyboard, printer, scanner and other devices
  5. Provides the user interface (desktop, icons, windows)
  6. Security – user accounts, passwords, permissions, updates

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: Name the Boolean operators used in literature search.
answer_html:
Boolean operators combine search terms:

  1. AND – retrieves records containing all the terms – narrows the search, e.g. diabetes AND foot care
  2. OR – retrieves records containing any of the terms – widens the search, e.g. bed sore OR pressure ulcer
  3. NOT – excludes records containing a term, e.g. asthma NOT children

Related techniques – phrase search with quotation marks ("hand hygiene") and truncation with an asterisk (nurs* = nurse, nurses, nursing).

Combined example – (hand hygiene OR hand washing) AND nurses NOT dentistry.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology

question: What is a computer virus? How can it be prevented?
answer_html:
Definition A computer virus is a harmful program that copies itself and spreads to other files or computers, damaging data or stealing information. It is one type of malware (along with worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware, which locks data and demands payment).

Prevention

  1. Install and regularly update antivirus software
  2. Keep the operating system and programs updated
  3. Do not open unknown e-mail attachments or links; avoid pirated software
  4. Scan pen drives before use
  5. Use a firewall and strong passwords
  6. Take regular backups of important data

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Introduction to Computer Applications in Nursing
question: What is e-learning? State its advantages.
answer_html:
Definition E-learning is learning through electronic media, mainly the internet and computers – online courses, video lectures, virtual classrooms, simulations and e-books.

Advantages

  1. Learn anytime, anywhere, at one's own pace
  2. Access to expert teachers and rich resources (videos, animations)
  3. Repeated revision of content; self-assessment quizzes with instant feedback
  4. Saves travel time and cost
  5. Useful for continuing education of working nurses (e.g. online CNE, MOOCs on SWAYAM)

Limitation – needs devices and internet; less hands-on practice and personal interaction.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define health informatics. Explain its need, objectives, components, applications and limitations.
answer_html:
Introduction Health care produces enormous amounts of data – histories, vital signs, test results, images, prescriptions and bills. Health informatics is the science of using this data wisely, with the help of information technology, to give safer, better and more efficient care and to improve public health.

A. Definition

  • Health informatics is the interdisciplinary field that deals with the collection, storage, retrieval, communication and optimal use of health data, information and knowledge, using information and communication technology, to support patient care, decision making, education, research and management
  • Nursing informatics is the specialty that integrates nursing science with information and computer sciences to manage and communicate data, information, knowledge and wisdom in nursing practice

B. Need (importance) of health informatics

  1. Huge volume of health data that cannot be managed on paper
  2. Need for quick access to complete patient information at the point of care
  3. Patient safety – reducing medication errors and missed results
  4. Continuity of care across hospitals, clinics and home (shared records)
  5. Evidence-based practice – rapid access to research and guidelines
  6. Efficient management – bed management, staffing, inventory, billing, quality monitoring
  7. Public health – disease surveillance, outbreak detection, planning of programmes
  8. Telehealth to reach rural and remote populations
  9. Digital health initiatives such as the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission

C. Objectives

  • To provide accurate, complete and timely information for clinical decisions
  • To improve the quality and safety of care
  • To reduce costs and duplication of tests
  • To support research, education and policy making
  • To promote communication and coordination among health workers
  • To empower patients with access to their own health information

D. Components

  1. Data – facts about patients, services and resources
  2. Hardware and software – computers, networks, applications
  3. People – health professionals, informaticians, IT staff, patients
  4. Processes and procedures – how data are collected, stored, used and protected
  5. Standards – terminologies and data-exchange standards (SNOMED CT, ICD, HL7)
  6. Policies and laws – privacy, security, consent

E. Applications

  • Electronic health records and hospital information systems
  • Clinical decision support (alerts, reminders, protocols)
  • Computerised physician order entry, eMAR and barcode medication administration
  • Telemedicine, telenursing and mobile health
  • Public health informatics – surveillance, registries, HMIS
  • Imaging informatics (PACS), laboratory information systems
  • Consumer health informatics – health apps, patient portals
  • Education (e-learning, simulation) and research (databases, analysis)

F. Limitations and challenges

  • High cost of setting up and maintaining systems; need for training
  • Lack of interoperability between different systems
  • Privacy and security risks – data breaches, cyber-attacks
  • Resistance to change among staff; increased documentation time initially
  • Infrastructure problems – power cuts, poor internet in rural areas
  • Errors caused by poor design, wrong data entry, copy-paste notes and alert fatigue
  • Digital divide – unequal access to technology

G. Development of health informatics (brief)

  • 1950s–1960s – computers used in hospitals mainly for billing and accounts
  • 1970s–1980s – hospital information systems, laboratory and pharmacy systems
  • 1992 – nursing informatics recognised as a nursing specialty in the USA
  • 2000s onwards – electronic health records, telemedicine, mobile health, data standards
  • India – EHR Standards (2013, revised 2016), National Digital Health Mission (2020), which became the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (2021) with ABHA health IDs and health registries

H. Role of the nurse in health informatics

  • Accurate and timely documentation – the quality of all information depends on correct data entry
  • Using information from records, dashboards and decision support to plan and evaluate care
  • Protecting privacy and security – passwords, logging out, sharing data only with authorised persons
  • Taking part in system selection, design, testing and training – nurses know the workflow best
  • Informatics nurse specialists – train staff, maintain nursing content (care plans, assessment forms), analyse data and lead projects
  • Reporting problems and safety issues related to technology

I. Future directions

  • AI-based decision support and predictive analytics
  • Nationwide interoperable health records linked to health IDs
  • Wider telehealth and remote monitoring with wearable devices
  • Use of genomic data for personalised care
  • Greater focus on cybersecurity and ethical use of data

Conclusion Health informatics is the use of information technology to collect, manage and use health data and knowledge; it is needed because of the volume of data and the demands of safety, continuity, efficiency and public health, and though it faces challenges of cost, interoperability, security and acceptance, it greatly improves care when used well.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the data–information–knowledge–wisdom (DIKW) framework with nursing examples.
answer_html:
Introduction The DIKW framework explains how raw facts are turned into wise decisions. In nursing informatics it shows how nurses use data to give care (described by Nelson and others).

1. Data

  • Raw, discrete facts without interpretation
  • Example – "38.9", "112", "24" (numbers recorded without context)

2. Information

  • Data that are organised, interpreted and given meaning
  • Example – "Temperature 38.9 °C, pulse 112/min, respiration 24/min in a patient on the second post-operative day"

3. Knowledge

  • Information that is combined, analysed and related to what is known, showing patterns and relationships
  • Example – the nurse recognises that fever, tachycardia and tachypnoea after surgery may indicate infection or sepsis

4. Wisdom

  • Appropriate use of knowledge to make decisions and act, considering the patient's situation and values
  • Example – the nurse inspects the wound, checks other signs, informs the doctor at once, sends a blood culture as ordered and increases monitoring

Characteristics

  • Moving from data to wisdom, the value and complexity increase
  • Computers handle data and information well; knowledge and wisdom depend on the nurse's education, experience and judgement, supported by decision-support systems

Importance in nursing

  • Accurate data entry is the foundation of good decisions
  • Shows the need for organised documentation and decision support
  • Basis for nursing informatics education and system design

Another example – blood glucose

  • Data – 320
  • Information – random blood glucose 320 mg/dL at 10 p.m. in a patient with type 2 diabetes on insulin
  • Knowledge – this is hyperglycaemia; possible causes are a missed insulin dose, infection or extra food; risk of ketoacidosis
  • Wisdom – the nurse checks for ketones and symptoms, reviews the medication chart, informs the doctor, gives insulin as ordered and teaches the patient

Role of computers at each level

  • Data – stored in databases and devices
  • Information – reports, graphs and trends generated automatically
  • Knowledge – guidelines, protocols and decision-support rules built into the system
  • Wisdom – remains the nurse's clinical judgement, supported but not replaced by technology

Conclusion In the DIKW framework, raw data become information when organised, knowledge when interpreted and related, and wisdom when applied appropriately; nurses move along this pathway every time they turn observations into safe clinical decisions.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the use of data and information for more effective health care and better health. Add a note on the qualities of good data.
answer_html:
Introduction Health care decisions – for one patient or for a whole country – are only as good as the data on which they are based. When data are collected well and converted into information, they lead to better care, better planning and better health.

1. Uses at different levels

  • Patient level – complete records help in diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and continuity of care; trends of vital signs or blood sugar guide treatment
  • Ward and hospital level – information on bed occupancy, infection rates, falls, pressure ulcers and medication errors helps nurse managers to plan staff, supplies and quality improvement
  • Programme and public health level – data from HMIS, disease surveillance and registries show disease trends, outbreaks and coverage of immunisation and maternal care; they guide planning and allocation of resources
  • Research and policy – large data sets reveal risk factors and the effectiveness of treatments; support evidence-based policies
  • Patients and communities – personal health records and health apps help people manage their own health

2. Qualities (dimensions) of good data

  • Accuracy – correct and free from errors
  • Completeness – no missing items
  • Timeliness – available when needed
  • Consistency – the same across records and systems
  • Validity – recorded in the correct format and within acceptable ranges
  • Relevance – useful for the purpose
  • Accessibility and confidentiality – available to authorised users only

3. Nurse's role

  • Record data accurately, completely and promptly, using standard terms
  • Use information from records, dashboards and reports to plan and evaluate care
  • Report problems in data systems; protect confidentiality

4. Example of data use

  • Monthly ward data show that most patient falls happen at night near the toilet
  • The team introduces hourly rounds, night lights, bed alarms and toilet assistance
  • Data over the next three months show a fall in the number of falls – information has led to better care

5. Barriers to effective use of data

  • Poor data quality (incomplete or late entries), lack of skills to analyse data, data kept in separate systems, delays in reports, and fear of blame when errors are reported

Conclusion Data, turned into information, improve care for individual patients, help hospitals manage and improve quality, and guide public health planning and research; this depends on data that are accurate, complete, timely, consistent, valid, relevant and secure.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the branches (types) of health informatics.
answer_html:
Introduction Health informatics has grown into several specialised branches, each applying information technology to a particular area of health care.

  1. Clinical informatics – use of information systems in direct patient care – EHR, CPOE, clinical decision support
  2. Nursing informatics – integration of nursing science with information science to support nursing practice, education, administration and research – electronic nursing documentation, care plans, standardised terminologies
  3. Medical informatics – focuses on doctors' clinical work, diagnosis and treatment decisions
  4. Public health informatics – use of information technology for population health – disease surveillance (e.g. IDSP), immunisation registries, HMIS, outbreak detection, GIS mapping
  5. Consumer health informatics – helping patients and the public to access and use health information – health websites, mobile apps, patient portals, wearable devices
  6. Imaging informatics – storage and sharing of X-rays, CT and MRI images (PACS, DICOM)
  7. Pharmacy informatics – electronic prescribing, drug databases, interaction checking, automated dispensing
  8. Laboratory informatics – laboratory information systems, automated reporting of results
  9. Bioinformatics – analysis of biological data such as genes and proteins (genomics)
  10. Dental informatics and veterinary informatics
  11. Translational and research informatics – managing data for clinical trials and research

Examples and the nurse's role

  • Clinical and nursing informatics – nurses document assessments, care plans and medicines in the EHR and use alerts and protocols
  • Public health informatics – ANMs and community health officers enter data on mothers, children, immunisation and TB patients into national portals (RCH portal, U-WIN, Nikshay); the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) supports disease surveillance
  • Consumer health informatics – nurses guide patients to reliable apps and websites and teach them to use personal health records
  • Imaging and laboratory informatics – nurses view results quickly and ensure correct patient identification on specimens and requests
  • Pharmacy informatics – nurses work with barcode scanning and automated dispensing cabinets
  • Research informatics – nurses collect and enter research data accurately and protect participants' privacy

Career roles for nurses – informatics nurse specialist, clinical application analyst, nursing data analyst, telehealth coordinator and EHR trainer.

All branches share the same goal – the right information, for the right person, at the right time.

Conclusion Health informatics includes clinical, nursing, medical, public health, consumer, imaging, pharmacy, laboratory, bioinformatics and research informatics, all aimed at using information to improve health and health care.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Differentiate between data and information.
answer_html:
Data Information
Raw, unprocessed facts and figures Processed, organised data with meaning
No context; meaningless by itself Has context and is useful for decisions
Example – 160, 100 Example – "BP 160/100 mmHg in a 45-year-old man – hypertension"
Input for processing Output of processing

Processing – data become information through collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting.

Knowledge – information analysed to show patterns and relationships, e.g. "persistent BP above 140/90 mmHg indicates hypertension needing treatment".

Data are the input; information is the output that is used for decisions.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is interoperability? Name its levels.
answer_html:
Definition Interoperability is the ability of different information systems, devices and applications to exchange data and use the exchanged data meaningfully – for example, a hospital system sending a discharge summary that a clinic's system can read and use.

Levels

  1. Foundational – data can be sent from one system to another
  2. Structural – the format (structure) of the data is standardised (e.g. HL7 messages)
  3. Semantic – the meaning is understood by both systems through common terminologies (e.g. SNOMED CT, LOINC)
  4. Organisational – policies, governance and trust that allow data sharing between organisations

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is big data in health care?
answer_html:
Definition Big data refers to extremely large and complex sets of data that cannot be handled by traditional methods and need advanced computing to store and analyse.

Characteristics (the "Vs") – volume (huge amount), velocity (generated rapidly), variety (records, images, sensor and genetic data), veracity (reliability) and value.

Sources – electronic health records, imaging, wearable devices, insurance claims, national programme databases, genomic data.

Uses – predicting disease outbreaks, identifying high-risk patients, improving hospital efficiency, research on treatment outcomes and personalised medicine.

Tools – data analytics, artificial intelligence and cloud computing.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is artificial intelligence (AI) in health care? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Artificial intelligence is the ability of computer systems to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence – learning from data, recognising patterns, understanding language and making predictions.

Examples in health care

  • Reading X-rays, CT scans and retinal photographs (e.g. diabetic retinopathy, tuberculosis screening)
  • Early warning systems that predict sepsis or patient deterioration
  • Chatbots and voice assistants for patient queries and reminders
  • Speech-to-text documentation, drug discovery, staffing predictions

Caution – AI must be used with human oversight; it may contain bias or errors, and patient privacy must be protected.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is nursing informatics? State its scope.
answer_html:
Definition Nursing informatics is the specialty that integrates nursing science with information and computer sciences to identify, collect, manage and communicate data, information, knowledge and wisdom in nursing practice.

Scope

  • Practice – electronic nursing documentation, care plans, eMAR, decision support, telenursing
  • Education – e-learning, simulation, informatics competencies
  • Administration – staffing, scheduling, quality indicators, resource management
  • Research – data collection and analysis, literature databases
  • System design – nurses help select, design, test and evaluate health information systems

Nursing informatics was recognised as a nursing specialty in 1992; informatics nurses act as a bridge between clinical staff and IT teams.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define hospital information system (HIS). Explain its objectives, modules, advantages, challenges and the role of the nurse.

diagram.caption: Modules of a hospital information system
labels: central patient database linked to registration and ADT

answer_html:
Introduction A modern hospital is a complex organisation with hundreds of patients, staff and departments working together every hour. A hospital information system (HIS) links all these activities through a common computer system, so that patient information, orders, results, medicines, bills and reports move quickly and accurately. In India, many public hospitals use systems such as e-Hospital, and private hospitals use commercial HIS software.

A. Definition

  • A hospital information system is a comprehensive, integrated computer-based system designed to manage the clinical, administrative and financial information of a hospital, so that the right information is available to the right person at the right time
  • It is also called a hospital management information system (HMIS)

B. Objectives

  1. To register and identify every patient with a unique number
  2. To make complete patient information available at the point of care
  3. To speed up communication of orders, results and reports
  4. To improve patient safety and quality of care
  5. To manage resources – beds, staff, drugs, equipment, finances
  6. To provide statistics and reports for management, planning and government reporting
  7. To reduce paperwork, duplication and cost

C. Modules (components) of HIS

1. Clinical modules

  • Patient registration and ADT – admission, discharge and transfer; bed management; unique hospital ID (UHID), linked with ABHA where available
  • Outpatient (OPD) module – appointments, queue management, consultation notes, e-prescriptions
  • Inpatient (IPD) and nursing module – nursing assessment, vital signs, care plans, nurses' notes, intake–output, handover
  • Electronic medical record – history, examination, diagnosis, progress notes, discharge summary
  • Order entry and results – laboratory, radiology and other investigations
  • Operation theatre – scheduling, surgical safety checklist, anaesthesia records
  • Emergency department, ICU and labour room modules

2. Ancillary / support modules

  • Laboratory information system (LIS) – sample tracking, barcoded labels, automated results
  • Radiology information system (RIS) and PACS – image storage and reporting
  • Pharmacy – drug stock, dispensing, expiry tracking, interaction checks
  • Blood bank, diet and kitchen, CSSD, laundry, biomedical waste

3. Administrative and financial modules

  • Billing and insurance (including government schemes such as PM-JAY), accounts
  • Inventory and stores, purchase
  • Human resources – staff records, duty rosters, payroll, attendance
  • Medical records department (MRD) – coding of diagnoses (ICD), storage and retrieval
  • Management information and reports – bed occupancy, mortality, infection rates, dashboards

D. Advantages

  • Quick access to complete, legible records from any authorised terminal
  • Fewer errors – no illegible handwriting; alerts for allergies and duplicate orders
  • Saves time – no carrying of files and slips; results available immediately
  • Better coordination between departments; reduced waiting time for patients
  • Accurate billing and control of stock and wastage
  • Data for quality improvement, research and government reporting
  • Continuity of care – previous records available on readmission

E. Challenges and disadvantages

  • High cost of hardware, software, maintenance and upgrades
  • Need for training and resistance to change among staff
  • Downtime – power or network failure stops work; backup procedures are needed
  • Data security and privacy risks – hacking, ransomware, misuse by insiders
  • Poorly designed screens may increase documentation time and cause errors
  • Lack of interoperability with other hospitals and systems

F. Role of the nurse

  • Use the system correctly – log in with one's own ID, document promptly and accurately, use standard terms
  • Verify patient identity before every entry, order or medicine
  • Protect confidentiality – never share passwords; log out; view only records needed for care
  • Report errors, system problems and safety concerns to the IT team and nurse manager
  • Follow downtime procedures – paper forms and later back-entry of data
  • Take part in selecting, testing and improving the nursing module; train new staff
  • Use HIS reports (falls, infections, pressure ulcers) for quality improvement

G. Steps in implementing an HIS

  1. Needs assessment – study the hospital's workflow, problems and goals
  2. Selection of the system or vendor; planning of budget and infrastructure (computers, network, power backup, servers or cloud)
  3. Customisation of forms, order sets and nursing modules with users' input
  4. Data migration of existing records; creation of master lists (drugs, tests, beds)
  5. Training of all users; appointment of "super-users" in each ward
  6. Pilot testing in a few departments, correction of problems
  7. Go-live with on-site support, followed by evaluation and continuous improvement

Conclusion A hospital information system is an integrated computer system that manages clinical, administrative and financial information through modules such as registration and ADT, OPD, IPD and nursing, laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, billing, stores and reports; it improves speed, safety and efficiency, but needs investment, training, security and good nursing use to succeed.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the clinical information system (CIS) and its components.
answer_html:
Introduction A clinical information system (CIS) is the part of the hospital's information system that directly supports patient care. It collects, stores and displays clinical data so that doctors, nurses and other professionals can make safe and timely decisions.

1. Definition

  • A CIS is a computer-based system that collects, stores, manipulates and makes available clinical information needed for patient care, at the bedside or anywhere in the hospital

2. Components

  • Electronic health/medical record (EHR/EMR) – history, problem list, allergies, progress notes, discharge summaries
  • Computerised provider order entry (CPOE) – doctors enter orders for medicines, tests and procedures electronically
  • Clinical decision support system (CDSS) – alerts for allergies, drug interactions and abnormal results; reminders; protocols
  • Electronic medication administration record (eMAR) and barcode medication administration – nurses scan the patient's wristband and the medicine before giving it
  • Nursing documentation system – assessments, care plans, vital signs, intake–output, early warning scores, handover reports
  • Laboratory information system (LIS) and radiology information system / PACS – results and images
  • Pharmacy information system – checking and dispensing prescriptions
  • Monitoring systems – data from bedside monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps transferred automatically
  • Specialty systems – ICU, operation theatre, emergency, maternity and oncology systems

3. Benefits

  • Real-time access to complete patient data
  • Fewer medication and transcription errors
  • Faster communication of orders and results
  • Trend displays (graphs of vital signs and laboratory values) help early detection of deterioration
  • Standardised care through order sets and protocols
  • Data for audits, quality improvement and research

4. Challenges

  • Alert fatigue, documentation burden, need for training, downtime, privacy risks

5. Nurse's role

  • Accurate and timely documentation, using decision support wisely, scanning every medicine, reporting system problems, and protecting confidentiality

6. Example of a CIS workflow

  • The doctor orders an IV antibiotic in CPOE; the system checks the patient's allergy record
  • The pharmacist verifies and dispenses it; the order appears on the nurse's eMAR
  • The nurse scans the wristband and the drug barcode before giving it; administration is recorded automatically with the time
  • Vital signs from the monitor are added to the chart; a critical laboratory result triggers an alert to the doctor and nurse

Conclusion A clinical information system supports direct patient care through the EHR, CPOE, decision support, eMAR with barcode scanning, nursing documentation, laboratory, radiology and pharmacy systems, giving faster, safer and better-coordinated care.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the role and architecture of information systems in modern health care.
answer_html:
Introduction An information system is an organised combination of people, hardware, software, data, networks and procedures that collects, processes, stores and distributes information to support decision making and control. In health care it connects every department and every level of care.

1. Role of information systems in modern health care

  • Clinical care – records, orders, results, decision support
  • Administration – registration, billing, staffing, stores, finance
  • Communication – between departments, hospitals, laboratories and patients
  • Quality and safety – incident reporting, infection surveillance, audits
  • Planning and policy – statistics for hospital and government planning
  • Research and education
  • Patient engagement – portals, appointments, reports on mobile phones

2. Components

  • Hardware – computers, servers, tablets, scanners, printers, monitors
  • Software – operating systems, HIS applications, databases
  • Data – stored in a database (organised collection of related data)
  • Network – LAN, Wi-Fi, internet, connecting users and systems
  • People – users (clinicians, nurses, clerks), IT staff, managers
  • Procedures – rules for use, security, backup and downtime

3. Types of architecture

  • Stand-alone systems – separate systems for each department (e.g. laboratory only) – simple but do not share data
  • Centralised (mainframe) architecture – one central computer serving many terminals
  • Client–server architecture – a central server stores data and applications; users' computers (clients) request and display information – common in hospitals
  • Web-based architecture – users access the system through a web browser
  • Cloud-based architecture – the system and data are hosted on remote servers provided over the internet; lower set-up cost, access from anywhere, but depends on internet and strong security
  • Integrated vs interfaced systems – an integrated system uses one common database; interfaced systems from different vendors exchange data through interfaces using standards such as HL7

4. Levels of information use

  • Operational – day-to-day tasks (admission, medicine administration)
  • Tactical – middle-level management (ward staffing, monthly stock)
  • Strategic – top management (planning new services, budgets)

5. Requirements of a good health information system

  • Reliable, fast, user-friendly, secure, interoperable, scalable, with backup and disaster recovery

Conclusion Information systems support care, administration, communication, quality and planning; they are made up of hardware, software, data, networks, people and procedures, and may be stand-alone, centralised, client–server, web-based or cloud-based, linked through standards such as HL7.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain computerised provider (physician) order entry (CPOE).
answer_html:
Introduction Handwritten orders are a major source of errors because of illegible handwriting, abbreviations, missing information and transcription mistakes. CPOE replaces handwritten orders with electronic orders entered directly into the computer.

1. Definition

  • Computerised provider order entry is a system that allows doctors and other authorised prescribers to enter medication, laboratory, radiology and other orders electronically, which are sent directly to the pharmacy, laboratory or nursing staff

2. Features

  • Structured order forms – drug name, dose, route, frequency and duration chosen from lists
  • Built-in clinical decision support – alerts for allergies, drug–drug interactions, duplicate orders and doses outside safe limits
  • Order sets – ready groups of orders for common conditions (e.g. a post-operative order set)
  • Weight-based dose calculation for children
  • Electronic signatures, date and time stamps

3. Advantages

  • Legible, complete orders – no handwriting errors
  • Fewer medication errors and adverse drug events
  • Faster delivery of orders to pharmacy and laboratory; quicker treatment
  • No transcription by nurses or clerks
  • Standardised, evidence-based care through order sets
  • Record of who ordered what and when (audit trail)

4. Disadvantages and risks

  • Alert fatigue – too many warnings lead to ignoring important ones
  • Selecting the wrong patient or wrong item from drop-down lists
  • Time-consuming at first; cost and training needs
  • Downtime – need for paper backup

5. Nurse's role

  • Review new orders promptly, check them against the patient's condition and clarify unclear or unsafe orders
  • Ensure verbal orders in emergencies are entered by the prescriber as soon as possible
  • Report problems with the system

6. Making CPOE work well

  • Involve doctors, nurses and pharmacists in designing screens and order sets
  • Keep the system simple and fast; limit alerts to important ones (tiered alerts) to prevent alert fatigue
  • Provide training and support during go-live
  • Monitor new types of error (wrong-patient orders, wrong drop-down selection) and correct the design
  • Studies have shown that well-designed CPOE with decision support significantly reduces serious medication errors

Conclusion CPOE allows prescribers to enter orders electronically with built-in safety checks, reducing errors, delays and transcription, but its benefits depend on good design, training and alertness to new types of error.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the laboratory information system (LIS) and the picture archiving and communication system (PACS).
answer_html:
Introduction Laboratory and imaging results form a large part of every patient's record. LIS and PACS manage these results electronically, making them faster, more accurate and easier to share.

A. Laboratory information system (LIS)

1. Definition – a computer system that manages the whole laboratory process, from the test request to the final report

2. Functions

  • Receives electronic test orders from the HIS/CPOE
  • Prints barcoded labels for specimen tubes – reduces mislabelling
  • Tracks specimens from collection to analysis
  • Interfaces with analysers – results are transferred automatically without manual typing
  • Quality control of tests; flags abnormal and critical values
  • Sends reports to the ward, doctor or patient electronically; stores results for trend comparison
  • Billing and laboratory statistics

3. Nurse's role – collect samples at the correct time, label at the bedside after scanning the wristband, send promptly, check results and report critical values immediately

B. PACS and RIS

1. Radiology information system (RIS) – manages radiology appointments, patient tracking, reporting and billing

2. PACS (picture archiving and communication system) – a system for storing, retrieving, displaying and sharing medical images (X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, mammography) digitally, without films

3. Components – imaging machines (modalities), secure network, image archive (servers), and viewing workstations; images use the DICOM standard

4. Advantages

  • No films or chemicals; images never lost
  • Images can be viewed at the same time by doctors in the ward, OT, ICU or another hospital (teleradiology)
  • Images can be enlarged, measured and compared with earlier studies
  • Faster reporting; saves storage space

5. Nurse's role – correct identification and preparation of patients, ensuring requests are complete, and accessing images and reports for care as authorised

C. Point-of-care testing and critical results

  • Bedside devices such as glucometers and blood gas analysers can send results directly to the LIS and the patient's record
  • Critical values (e.g. very high potassium, very low glucose) are flagged; the laboratory telephones the ward, and the nurse reads back the result, records the time and informs the doctor at once

Conclusion The laboratory information system manages test orders, barcoded specimens, automated results and reports, while RIS and PACS manage radiology workflow and store and share digital images using the DICOM standard; both speed up care and reduce errors.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is HL7?
answer_html:
HL7 (Health Level Seven) is a set of international standards for the exchange of clinical and administrative data between health information systems, developed by HL7 International (founded 1987).

  • "Level Seven" refers to the seventh (application) layer of the computer networking model
  • Versions – HL7 version 2 messages (widely used for admissions, orders and results), version 3 and the Clinical Document Architecture (CDA), and the modern web-based FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources)
  • Use – allows, for example, the HIS to send a laboratory order to the LIS and receive the result back automatically

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Name the types of information systems used in health care organisations.
answer_html:
1. Transaction processing system (TPS) – records routine daily transactions – registration, billing, stock issues
  2. Management information system (MIS) – produces regular reports for middle managers – monthly bed occupancy, staff attendance
  3. Decision support system (DSS) – helps managers and clinicians analyse options and make decisions (clinical decision support is a type)
  4. Executive information system (EIS) – gives summaries and dashboards to top management for strategic planning
  5. Expert system – uses a knowledge base and rules to give expert-like advice (e.g. diagnostic support)
  6. Office automation systems – word processing, e-mail, scheduling

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is an ADT system?
answer_html:
ADT (Admission, Discharge and Transfer) system is the core module of a hospital information system that records and tracks the patient's movement through the hospital.

Functions

  • Registration and allotment of a unique hospital number (UHID)
  • Admission – ward, bed, consultant, diagnosis
  • Transfer between wards, ICU and operation theatre
  • Discharge – date, time, type of discharge, summary
  • Bed management – real-time display of occupied, vacant and reserved beds
  • Provides data for census, bed occupancy and billing; patient details are shared with all other modules

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What are downtime procedures in a hospital information system?
answer_html:
Downtime is a period when the computer system is unavailable – planned (maintenance, upgrade) or unplanned (power failure, network failure, cyber-attack).

Downtime procedures

  1. Switch to paper forms – medication charts, order sheets, laboratory requests, nursing notes (kept ready on every ward)
  2. Use printed downtime reports (patient list, current medications, allergies) prepared in advance
  3. Communicate by telephone; follow the hospital's emergency plan
  4. When the system returns, enter the paper data into the computer (back-entry) and file the paper records
  5. Report the event and review it afterwards

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is PACS?
answer_html:
PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) is a computer system for storing, retrieving, displaying and sharing medical images such as X-rays, CT, MRI and ultrasound in digital form, replacing films.

Components – imaging machines, a secure network, an image archive and viewing workstations; images use the DICOM standard.

Advantages – no films or chemicals; images available instantly in wards, ICU and OT; comparison with old images; teleradiology (reporting from a distance); less storage space.

Limitations – high cost, need for large storage and fast networks, and dependence on the system (downtime).

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: Define electronic health record (EHR). Explain its components, functions, advantages, challenges and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Traditionally, a patient's information was scattered in paper files in different hospitals and clinics – often lost, illegible or unavailable when needed. The electronic health record (EHR) brings the patient's information together in digital form so that it can follow the patient across settings and over a lifetime. It is the foundation of digital health, including India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.

A. Definition

  • An electronic health record is a digital, longitudinal record of a person's health information, created and shared by authorised health care providers across different organisations, containing the patient's medical history, diagnoses, medicines, allergies, test results, immunisations and treatment plans
  • It is patient-centred and lifelong, unlike an EMR which is limited to one organisation

B. Components (contents)

  • Demographic data – name, age, sex, address, unique ID (e.g. ABHA number)
  • Medical history, problem list and diagnoses
  • Allergies and alerts
  • Medication list and prescriptions
  • Immunisation records
  • Laboratory results, imaging reports and images
  • Clinical notes – doctors' and nurses' notes, assessments, care plans, vital signs
  • Procedures and surgeries, discharge summaries, referral letters
  • Consent forms and advance directives
  • Administrative and billing data

C. Core functions (as described by the Institute of Medicine)

  1. Health information and data – store and display the patient's data
  2. Results management – electronic access to current and past test results
  3. Order management – electronic orders (CPOE)
  4. Decision support – alerts, reminders, guidelines
  5. Electronic communication and connectivity – among providers and with patients
  6. Patient support – patient education, access to own records
  7. Administrative processes – scheduling, billing, insurance
  8. Reporting and population health – reports for quality and public health

D. Advantages

  • Complete, legible and up-to-date information at the point of care
  • Continuity of care across hospitals, clinics and home; fewer repeated tests
  • Patient safety – allergy and interaction alerts, fewer lost results
  • Faster communication and coordination among the team
  • Efficient – less paper, storage space and time spent searching files
  • Data for research, quality improvement and public health
  • Patient empowerment – patients can view their records through personal health record apps

E. Challenges

  • Capturing rich patient histories in computable form – much important information (the patient's story, social situation, nursing observations) is in free text that computers cannot easily analyse; structured forms and coding take more time and may miss detail
  • Copy-and-paste notes and templates may carry forward outdated or wrong information
  • Interoperability – systems from different vendors may not exchange data
  • Cost, infrastructure (power, internet) and training needs
  • Privacy and security – risk of breaches and misuse
  • Data entry burden – less time with patients if systems are poorly designed
  • Legal and ethical issues – consent, ownership and access rights

F. Role of the nurse

  • Document accurately, objectively and promptly – "if it is not documented, it was not done"
  • Use standardised terminologies and structured forms where available, adding clear narrative notes
  • Verify patient identity and review the record before care
  • Avoid copy-paste errors; correct errors as per policy (the system keeps an audit trail)
  • Protect confidentiality – own login, log out, access only what is needed
  • Teach patients about their health ID and personal health record
  • Participate in EHR design, testing and training

G. Principles of documentation in an EHR

  • Accurate and objective – record facts, not opinions; quote the patient's words where useful
  • Timely – document as soon as possible after care; label late entries clearly
  • Complete and concise – all assessments, interventions and responses, without unnecessary repetition
  • Use approved terms and abbreviations only
  • Corrections are made through the system's amendment function – the original entry and the change are kept in the audit trail; never delete or alter another person's entry
  • Never document for another person and never share login details

H. EHR adoption in India

  • Many government hospitals use e-Hospital or state hospital management systems; private hospitals use commercial EHRs
  • ABDM links records from different facilities through the ABHA health ID with patient consent
  • Challenges include uneven infrastructure, training needs, multiple languages and paper-based practices in smaller facilities, which are gradually being addressed

Conclusion The electronic health record is a lifelong, shareable digital record of a person's health information containing demographics, history, medicines, allergies, results, notes and plans; it supports results and order management, decision support, communication and reporting, improving continuity and safety, but faces challenges of computable documentation, interoperability, cost and privacy, in which nurses play a central role.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: Explain the standards and recent developments that enable lifelong electronic health records to be integrated from different systems. Add a note on the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM).
answer_html:
Introduction A lifelong health record is possible only when data from many different systems – hospitals, clinics, laboratories, pharmacies and mobile apps – can be combined and understood. This requires common standards for the structure, meaning, exchange and security of data, and a national digital framework.

PART A – TYPES OF STANDARDS

1. Data exchange (messaging) standards

  • HL7 version 2 – messages for admission, orders and results between hospital systems
  • HL7 CDA (Clinical Document Architecture) – standard structure for clinical documents such as discharge summaries
  • HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) – a modern, web-based standard that exchanges small units of data ("resources" such as Patient, Observation, Medication) using internet technologies; widely adopted worldwide and in India's digital health systems
  • DICOM – standard for medical images and their exchange
  • IHE profiles – guidance on how to use standards together in real workflows

2. Terminology and coding standards (meaning)

  • SNOMED CT – comprehensive clinical terminology for diagnoses, findings, procedures; India has a national release centre and free national use
  • LOINC – codes for laboratory tests and clinical observations
  • ICD-10 / ICD-11 – WHO classification of diseases for statistics and billing (ICD-11 in use from 2022)
  • Drug codes, and nursing terminologies (NANDA-I, NIC, NOC)

3. Record architecture standards

  • ISO 13606 and openEHR – models (archetypes) that define the structure of EHR content so that it can be shared and kept for a lifetime independent of software

4. Security and privacy standards

  • Authentication, access control, encryption, audit trails, consent management; ISO standards for information security

PART B – GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS

  • Many countries have national EHR or health information exchange systems with unique patient identifiers
  • Patient portals and personal health records allow people to see and share their own records
  • FHIR-based application interfaces (APIs) allow apps to connect securely to records
  • Cloud platforms and mobile health make records accessible anywhere
  • Growing use of artificial intelligence on large, standardised data sets

PART C – INDIA: EHR STANDARDS

  • The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified EHR Standards for India in 2013, revised in 2016, recommending standards such as ISO 13606/openEHR, HL7, DICOM, SNOMED CT, LOINC and ICD-10, with guidance on minimum data sets, privacy and record retention

PART D – AYUSHMAN BHARAT DIGITAL MISSION (ABDM)

1. Background – launched as the National Digital Health Mission in 2020 and as ABDM in 2021, implemented by the National Health Authority; it aims to create an integrated digital health ecosystem for the country

2. Building blocks

  • ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) number – a 14-digit unique health ID for every citizen, with an easy ABHA address; used to link health records from different providers
  • Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR) – verified registry of doctors, nurses and other professionals
  • Health Facility Registry (HFR) – registry of public and private hospitals, clinics, laboratories and pharmacies
  • Health Information Exchange and Consent Manager – records are shared only with the patient's consent, through a consent manager
  • Personal Health Record (PHR) apps – e.g. the ABHA app, where people store and view their records
  • Unified Health Interface for digital services (appointments, teleconsultation) and the National Health Claims Exchange for insurance claims
  • "Scan and Share" – QR-code-based quick OPD registration using ABHA

3. Benefits

  • Lifelong, portable records; fewer repeated tests; faster registration
  • Patient control through consent; continuity of care across public and private sectors
  • Better data for planning and research

4. Role of the nurse

  • Help patients create ABHA and link records; explain consent and privacy
  • Register in the HPR; document using standards; protect confidentiality

PART E – Benefits of standards

  • Data can move between systems without being retyped, reducing errors
  • The same meaning is understood by every system (semantic interoperability)
  • Records remain readable for a lifetime, even when software changes
  • National statistics, research and public health reporting become possible
  • Patients can choose providers freely and carry their records with them

PART F – Nurse's role

  • Use standard terms and nursing terminologies (NANDA-I, NIC, NOC) in documentation
  • Complete structured fields (allergies, vital signs, medications) carefully – they are the data that move between systems
  • Take part in selecting and testing systems that follow national standards

Conclusion Lifelong integrated health records depend on exchange standards (HL7, CDA, FHIR, DICOM), terminology standards (SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD), record architecture (ISO 13606, openEHR) and security standards; in India the EHR Standards of 2016 and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, with ABHA, professional and facility registries, consent-based exchange and PHR apps, are building this integrated system.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: Differentiate between electronic medical record (EMR), electronic health record (EHR) and personal health record (PHR).
answer_html:
Introduction The terms EMR, EHR and PHR are often confused. They differ mainly in who creates and controls the record and how widely it is shared.

Point EMR EHR PHR
Meaning Digital version of the patient's chart in one organisation Digital, comprehensive and shareable record across organisations Record managed by the patient (or family)
Created by Clinicians of one hospital or clinic Many providers, contributing to one record The patient, with data from providers and devices
Controlled by The organisation Providers, with patient consent The patient
Scope One episode or one facility Lifelong, across settings Lifelong; may include diet, exercise, wearable data
Sharing Limited to the facility Shared among authorised providers Shared by the patient as he chooses
Example A hospital's own record system Records linked through ABHA under ABDM ABHA app, fitness apps, diabetes diary apps

Main points

  • An EMR helps one organisation give care; an EHR supports continuity of care among many; a PHR empowers patients to manage their own health
  • All three need accuracy, security and standards

Nurse's role – document accurately in the EMR/EHR, and teach patients to maintain and use their PHR (medicines, reports, appointments)

Explanation

  • EMR – the electronic version of the paper chart of one hospital or clinic; used for diagnosis and treatment within that organisation; usually not easily shared outside it, so information may be lost when the patient moves to another provider
  • EHR – brings together information from all providers involved in a person's care; designed to be shared with authorised clinicians across organisations, using common standards; supports continuity, referrals and public health reporting
  • PHR – kept by the patient; may include records downloaded from providers, self-measured readings (BP, blood sugar, weight), medicines, appointments and data from fitness devices; helps patients take part in their care, but its accuracy depends on the patient and it may not be complete
  • Patient portals – secure websites or apps through which patients can see parts of their EHR, book appointments and receive reports

Conclusion The EMR is an organisation's digital chart, the EHR is a lifelong record shared across providers, and the PHR is a record controlled by the patient; together they support coordinated, patient-centred care.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: Explain shared care and the role of electronic records in supporting it.
answer_html:
Introduction Many patients, especially those with chronic diseases, are cared for by several providers – a hospital specialist, a primary health centre, a community health worker, a pharmacist and the family. Shared care means these providers work together using shared information.

1. Definition

  • Shared care is an arrangement in which responsibility for a patient's care is shared between two or more providers or settings, with agreed plans, clear roles and exchange of information

2. Examples

  • Diabetes or hypertension – diagnosed and stabilised by a specialist, followed up at a health and wellness centre by a community health officer and ANM
  • Antenatal care – between the PHC and the district hospital
  • Tuberculosis – diagnosis at a centre, treatment supervision in the community (Nikshay records)
  • Mental health, cancer care, palliative care, post-discharge home care

3. Requirements

  • Agreed care plans and protocols
  • Clear roles and communication between providers
  • Shared, up-to-date information – the most important requirement
  • Patient and family involvement

4. Role of electronic records

  • A common EHR or linked records (e.g. through ABHA) let all providers see the same history, medicines, allergies and results
  • Electronic referrals and discharge summaries reach the next provider immediately
  • Alerts and reminders for follow-up visits and tests
  • Telemedicine links specialists with primary care
  • Patient portals/PHR apps allow patients to carry their information

5. Challenges

  • Systems that do not communicate, incomplete records, unclear responsibility, privacy concerns, poor internet in rural areas

6. Nurse's role

  • Prepare clear discharge summaries and referral notes, including nursing problems and teaching given
