  • Coordinate follow-up; educate patients and families; update records promptly

7. Example

  • A pregnant woman with gestational diabetes is managed jointly by the district hospital obstetrician, the PHC medical officer and the ANM
  • Blood sugar readings, scan reports and the treatment plan are available to all through linked records; the ANM sees the plan and reinforces diet and insulin teaching at home visits
  • After delivery, the discharge summary is sent electronically to the PHC for postnatal follow-up and screening for diabetes

Conclusion Shared care divides responsibility for a patient among several providers with agreed plans and roles, and electronic records, referrals, discharge summaries and personal health records make it safe and continuous.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: Explain the challenges of capturing patient histories in computable form. Add a note on structured and unstructured data.
answer_html:
Introduction A patient's history is a rich story – symptoms, feelings, family and social situation, beliefs and nursing observations. For computers to analyse, share and use this information (for alerts, research or exchange), it must be recorded in a computable (structured and coded) form. Doing this without losing meaning is a major challenge of EHRs.

1. Structured and unstructured data

  • Structured data – recorded in fixed fields, drop-down lists, check boxes and codes (e.g. BP 140/90; allergy: penicillin – coded; diagnosis coded with ICD or SNOMED CT); easy for computers to search, analyse and exchange
  • Unstructured data – free text (narrative notes, history in the patient's words), scanned documents, images, audio; rich in detail but hard for computers to use

2. Challenges

  • Loss of the patient's story – tick boxes may miss important details and context
  • Time and effort – structured entry is slow; clinicians may skip fields
  • Complex terminologies – choosing the correct code from thousands is difficult; wrong codes create wrong information
  • Variation in terms used by different professionals
  • Copy-and-paste and templates may record findings that were not actually examined
  • Old paper records need scanning, which produces unstructured images
  • Language – patients' descriptions in local languages
  • Interoperability – different systems use different structures and codes

3. Solutions

  • Balanced documentation – structured fields for key data (allergies, vital signs, medicines, problems) plus narrative notes for the story
  • Standard terminologies (SNOMED CT, LOINC, NANDA-I/NIC/NOC) built into easy pick-lists
  • Well-designed templates that follow the clinical workflow
  • Natural language processing to extract coded data from free text
  • Voice recognition to reduce typing
  • Training and regular audits of documentation quality

Nurse's role – complete structured fields accurately, add clear narrative notes, and avoid copy-paste errors

Example – an allergy written in free text ("patient allergic to sulpha drugs") cannot trigger an alert, but the same allergy recorded as a coded entry ("sulfonamide allergy") automatically warns the doctor and nurse when a sulfonamide is prescribed.

Conclusion Capturing patient histories in computable form requires structured, coded data that computers can use, without losing the meaning held in free-text narratives; well-designed templates, standard terminologies, new technology and careful documentation help overcome these challenges.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: What is ABHA?
answer_html:
ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) is a 14-digit unique health identification number created under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission for every Indian resident who wishes to have one.

  • It comes with an easy-to-remember ABHA address (like an e-mail ID)
  • It links a person's health records from different hospitals, laboratories and clinics
  • Records are shared only with the person's consent
  • It can be created free using Aadhaar, a driving licence or mobile number through the ABHA app or website, or at a health facility
  • It enables quick registration (e.g. "Scan and Share" in OPDs)

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: What is FHIR?
answer_html:
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is a modern standard from HL7 International for exchanging health information electronically.

  • Data are exchanged as small, reusable units called "resources" – e.g. Patient, Observation, Medication, Appointment
  • Uses common web technologies (APIs, JSON/XML), so it is easier and faster to implement than older standards
  • Allows mobile apps, EHRs and national health platforms to connect securely
  • Widely used worldwide and in digital health systems in India

Example – a diabetes app on the patient's phone fetches the latest HbA1c result from the hospital record through a FHIR interface.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: What is health information exchange (HIE)?
answer_html:
Health information exchange is the electronic sharing of health information among different organisations – hospitals, clinics, laboratories, pharmacies and public health agencies – in a secure and standardised way.

Benefits – the patient's records are available wherever he goes, fewer repeated tests, faster referrals, better continuity of care and public health reporting.

Requirements – common standards (HL7, FHIR, SNOMED CT), unique patient identification, patient consent, security and legal framework. In India it is provided through ABDM's Health Information Exchange and Consent Manager.

Models – centralised (one central database), federated (data stay with each provider and are fetched when needed) and hybrid.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Shared Care and Electronic Health Records
question: What is a consent manager in digital health?
answer_html:
A consent manager is a digital service that allows a person to give, view, manage and withdraw consent for sharing his health records between providers.

Features

  • The patient receives a request (who wants the data, for what purpose, which records, for how long)
  • He can approve or deny it on his mobile phone; consent can be time-limited and withdrawn
  • Records move only after consent; every access is recorded

Use – the core privacy safeguard in ABDM's health information exchange.

The consent manager does not store the health records itself; it only manages the permissions for sharing them.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the relationship between patient safety and informatics. Describe how health information technology improves patient safety and the new risks it can introduce.
answer_html:
Introduction Patient safety means the prevention of errors and avoidable harm to patients during health care. Every year many patients are harmed by medication errors, infections, falls, misidentification and delayed diagnosis. Many of these errors are linked to poor information – illegible orders, missing results, incomplete handovers. Health informatics improves the flow of information and therefore has a close relationship with safety. The WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan 2021–2030 and India's National Patient Safety Implementation Framework both encourage the safe use of digital tools; World Patient Safety Day is observed on 17 September.

PART A – RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN PATIENT SAFETY AND INFORMATICS

  1. Errors are often information failures – wrong patient, wrong drug, missed allergy, lost result, poor handover
  2. Informatics provides the right information at the right time – complete records, alerts and reminders at the point of care
  3. Standardisation – electronic order sets, protocols and checklists reduce variation
  4. Measurement – electronic data allow monitoring of safety indicators (falls, infections, pressure injuries, medication errors)
  5. Learning – electronic incident reporting and analysis help organisations learn from errors
  6. But technology can also create new errors if poorly designed or used – safety must be designed into systems

PART B – HEALTH INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY THAT IMPROVES SAFETY

1. Computerised provider order entry (CPOE) – legible, complete orders; no transcription; built-in checks for dose and duplication

2. Clinical decision support (CDSS) – alerts for allergies, drug–drug interactions, renal dose adjustment, abnormal results; reminders for prophylaxis and screening

3. Barcode medication administration (BCMA) with eMAR – scanning of the patient's wristband and the medicine confirms the right patient, drug, dose, route and time before administration

4. Smart infusion pumps – built-in drug libraries with dose limits (dose error reduction systems) prevent programming errors with high-alert drugs

5. Electronic early warning scores – automatic calculation of scores such as NEWS2 from vital signs to detect deterioration and sepsis early and alert the rapid response team

6. Positive patient identification – barcoded or RFID wristbands, photographs in the record, two-identifier prompts

7. Electronic health records – complete history, allergy list and problem list available to all; fewer lost files

8. Laboratory systems – barcoded specimen labels, automatic notification of critical values

9. Automated dispensing cabinets and pharmacy systems – controlled access to medicines, stock and expiry tracking

10. Electronic handover tools (e.g. SBAR templates), risk assessment tools built into documentation (fall risk, pressure injury risk), infection surveillance systems and telemetry

11. Electronic incident reporting systems – easy, quick reporting and analysis of incidents and near misses

PART C – NEW RISKS INTRODUCED BY TECHNOLOGY (e-iatrogenesis)

  • Wrong-patient errors – selecting the wrong patient or the wrong item from drop-down lists
  • Alert fatigue – too many alerts cause users to ignore important warnings
  • Copy-and-paste documentation carrying forward outdated or wrong information
  • Workarounds – e.g. scanning a spare copy of a wristband instead of the patient's own, bypassing safety checks
  • Automation bias – over-trusting the computer and not using clinical judgement
  • Interface and data errors – results attached to the wrong patient, incorrect unit conversions
  • Downtime – loss of access to records during power or network failure
  • Cyber-attacks and ransomware – can stop hospital services and expose patient data
  • Usability problems – confusing screens, too many clicks, small fonts
  • Reduced face-to-face communication among team members

PART D – MEASURES TO MAKE TECHNOLOGY SAFE

  • User-centred design with input from nurses and doctors; testing before use
  • Tiered, relevant alerts to reduce alert fatigue
  • Training and competency checks; clear policies prohibiting workarounds
  • Downtime procedures and regular backups; cybersecurity measures
  • Monitoring and reporting of technology-related incidents; regular system updates
  • Maintaining clinical judgement and direct communication

PART E – ROLE OF THE NURSE

  • Use safety technology every time (e.g. scan every medicine); never bypass checks
  • Read and respond to alerts thoughtfully; report unhelpful alerts
  • Ensure correct patient selection and accurate data entry
  • Report technology-related errors and near misses
  • Take part in design, testing and training; educate patients about safe use of health apps

Conclusion Patient safety and informatics are closely linked because most errors are information failures; CPOE, decision support, barcode medication administration, smart pumps, early warning systems, electronic records and incident reporting prevent harm, but technology can also cause new errors such as wrong-patient selection, alert fatigue, copy-paste errors, workarounds and downtime, so it must be designed, used and monitored carefully, with nurses playing a central role.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define clinical risk management. Explain the steps of the risk management process and its functions and applications in nursing.

diagram.caption: Risk management process
labels: with communication and consultation around the cycle

answer_html:
Introduction Health care involves many risks – medication errors, falls, infections, pressure injuries, equipment failures and miscommunication. Clinical risk management is a systematic way of finding these risks before they cause harm, reducing them, and learning from incidents. It protects patients, staff and the organisation.

PART A – DEFINITIONS

  • Hazard – anything with the potential to cause harm (e.g. a wet floor, a look-alike drug)
  • Risk – the chance (likelihood) that a hazard will cause harm, combined with the severity (consequence) of that harm
  • Risk management – coordinated activities to identify, assess, control and monitor risks
  • Clinical risk management – risk management applied to clinical care, aiming to reduce avoidable harm to patients and improve the quality and safety of care

PART B – STEPS OF THE RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS

1. Establishing the context

  • Define the area (e.g. a medical ward), objectives, responsibilities and criteria for judging risk

2. Risk identification – finding what can go wrong, using:

  • Incident and near-miss reports
  • Audits (documentation, hand hygiene, medication charts)
  • Patient complaints and feedback; legal claims
  • Morbidity and mortality reviews
  • Trigger tools – reviewing records for "triggers" such as use of naloxone or transfer to ICU
  • Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) – a proactive step-by-step study of a process (e.g. blood transfusion) to find possible failures
  • Walk-rounds, staff suggestions, data from information systems (falls, infections, pressure ulcers)

3. Risk analysis

  • Estimate the likelihood (rare to almost certain) and the consequence (insignificant to catastrophic)
  • Use a risk matrix: risk score = likelihood × consequence, giving low, moderate, high or extreme risk

4. Risk evaluation

  • Compare the risk with acceptable levels; prioritise risks
  • Record them in a risk register with the owner, actions and review dates

5. Risk treatment (control)

  • Avoid – stop the risky activity (e.g. remove concentrated potassium chloride from ward stock)
  • Reduce – introduce controls (barcode scanning, double checks, bed alarms, hourly rounds, training)
  • Transfer – share the risk (insurance, outsourcing to specialists)
  • Accept – where the risk is low and controls are not practical, with monitoring
  • Use the hierarchy of controls – elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls (policies, training), personal protective equipment

6. Monitoring and review

  • Check that controls are working (audits, indicators, re-scoring of risks); update the register

7. Communication and consultation – throughout the process, with staff, patients and management

PART C – FUNCTIONS OF CLINICAL RISK MANAGEMENT

  • Prevent harm to patients and staff
  • Learn from incidents and share lessons
  • Improve quality and reliability of care
  • Legal and financial protection – reduce claims and losses
  • Support accreditation (e.g. NABH) and compliance with standards
  • Build a safety culture (open reporting, just culture)

PART D – APPLICATIONS IN NURSING

  • Falls – risk assessment on admission, bed height, call bell, non-slip footwear, bed alarms, hourly rounds
  • Pressure injuries – risk scoring, repositioning, support surfaces
  • Medication safety – rights, double checks for high-alert drugs, barcode scanning, safe storage
  • Healthcare-associated infections – hand hygiene audits, care bundles for catheters and lines
  • Patient identification – wristbands, two identifiers before procedures and transfusion
  • Restraint and seclusion – policies and monitoring
  • Equipment – maintenance, checking defibrillators and suction daily
  • Communication – structured handover (SBAR), read-back of verbal orders
  • Self-harm risk in mental health and emergency settings – assessment and safe environment

PART E – ROLE OF INFORMATICS

  • Electronic incident reporting and analysis, electronic risk registers
  • Dashboards showing safety indicators in real time
  • Alerts based on risk scores (e.g. high fall risk flagged on the patient list)
  • Data analysis to detect trends and evaluate controls

PART F – Example of a ward risk assessment

  • Risk – falls among elderly patients at night
  • Analysis – likelihood "likely" (score 4) × consequence "major" (score 4) = 16 – high risk
  • Controls – fall-risk assessment on admission, low beds, bed alarms, night lights, non-slip footwear, hourly rounding, toilet assistance, review of sedatives
  • Re-assessment after three months – likelihood reduced to "possible" (2) × major (4) = 8 – moderate; continue monitoring

PART G – Just culture

  • Honest mistakes are treated as system problems and lead to learning, while reckless behaviour is dealt with fairly; this encourages staff to report incidents and risks openly

Conclusion Clinical risk management is the systematic identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment and monitoring of risks in clinical care, supported by communication and a just culture; nurses apply it daily to falls, pressure injuries, medicines, infections, identification and equipment, and informatics makes reporting, analysis and monitoring faster and more effective.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain incident reporting systems in health care.
answer_html:
Introduction An incident reporting system allows staff to report errors, near misses and unsafe conditions so that the organisation can learn and prevent recurrence. It is a cornerstone of patient safety and risk management.

1. Definitions

  • Incident – any unplanned event that caused or could have caused harm to a patient, visitor or staff member
  • Near miss – an error that did not reach the patient (caught in time) or reached the patient without harm
  • Adverse event – an incident that caused harm to the patient due to care rather than the disease
  • Sentinel event – an unexpected event causing death or serious harm, needing immediate investigation
  • Never events – serious, largely preventable events that should never happen (e.g. wrong-site surgery, retained swab, wrong-route administration)

2. What should be reported

  • Medication errors, falls, pressure injuries, patient misidentification, wrong blood transfusion
  • Equipment failure, infections, delays in treatment, violence, needle-stick injuries
  • Unsafe conditions (e.g. broken equipment, staffing shortages)

3. How to report

  • As soon as possible, through the hospital's paper or electronic form
  • Facts only – what happened, when, where, who was involved (without blame), the immediate action and the outcome
  • Inform the nurse in charge and the doctor; care for the patient first
  • The incident report is not filed in the patient's record, but the clinical facts are documented in the notes

4. Characteristics of a good reporting system

  • Non-punitive – staff are not punished for honest reporting (just culture)
  • Confidential, simple and quick (electronic forms)
  • Timely analysis by trained people; focus on systems, not individuals
  • Feedback to reporters and sharing of lessons learnt

5. Benefits

  • Identifies hazards and patterns; prevents recurrence; improves quality; supports accreditation; builds a safety culture

6. Role of informatics – electronic reporting from any terminal, automatic notification of managers, classification, trend analysis and dashboards

7. Example of a factual report entry "At 10.15 p.m. on 14/11, the patient in bed 12 was found sitting on the floor beside the bed. He said he slipped while going to the toilet alone. No visible injury; BP 130/80, pulse 84. Doctor informed at 10.20 p.m.; patient assisted to bed; bed lowered and call bell placed within reach."

Conclusion Incident reporting systems capture incidents, near misses, adverse events and sentinel events in a factual, non-punitive and confidential way, allowing analysis and learning that prevent future harm.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain barcode medication administration (BCMA).
answer_html:
Introduction Medication administration is the last step before a medicine reaches the patient, so errors here are rarely caught. Barcode medication administration uses scanning to confirm the rights of medication administration electronically at the bedside.

1. Definition

  • BCMA is a system in which the nurse scans the barcode on the patient's wristband and on the medication with a handheld scanner before giving a drug; the computer checks the scan against the electronic medication administration record (eMAR)

2. Components

  • Barcoded patient wristbands
  • Barcoded unit-dose medicines (labelled by the manufacturer or pharmacy)
  • Handheld scanners or mobile devices, linked by Wi-Fi
  • eMAR connected to CPOE and pharmacy systems
  • Nurse's ID badge barcode for login

3. Steps

  1. Nurse logs in and opens the patient's eMAR
  2. Scans the patient's wristband – confirms the right patient
  3. Scans each medicine – the system checks the right drug, dose, route, time and alerts for allergies or early doses
  4. Gives the medicine if there is no alert; the administration is recorded automatically with date and time
  5. Documents the reason for any dose not given

4. Advantages

  • Reduces wrong-patient, wrong-drug, wrong-dose and wrong-time errors
  • Automatic, accurate documentation; no illegible charts
  • Alerts for allergies and look-alike drugs
  • Data on missed or late doses for quality monitoring

5. Problems and workarounds to avoid

  • Damaged or missing barcodes; scanner or Wi-Fi failures
  • Workarounds – scanning a spare wristband stuck on the bed or chart, overriding alerts without thinking, scanning several medicines for several patients at once
  • Nurses must always scan at the bedside, one patient at a time, and report problems

6. Requirements for successful BCMA

  • Medicines supplied in barcoded unit-dose packs (pharmacy re-labelling where needed)
  • Reliable Wi-Fi, enough scanners and a back-up plan for breakdowns
  • Training of nurses and clear policies on when alerts may be overridden
  • Regular review of override rates and scanning compliance as quality indicators

Conclusion Barcode medication administration confirms the right patient and medicine at the bedside by scanning the wristband and drug against the eMAR, reducing errors and improving documentation, provided nurses use it correctly without workarounds.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain root cause analysis (RCA).
answer_html:
Introduction When a serious incident occurs, it is not enough to blame an individual. Root cause analysis looks deeply into why the event happened so that the underlying system problems can be fixed.

1. Definition

  • RCA is a structured, retrospective method of investigating an incident to identify its root causes – the basic reasons which, if removed, would prevent the event from happening again

2. When it is used – sentinel events, never events, serious adverse events and repeated incidents

3. Steps

  1. Form a team – people with knowledge of the process (nurses, doctors, pharmacist, quality officer), not directly blamed
  2. Collect information – records, statements, observation of the area, equipment, policies
  3. Describe what happened – a timeline or flowchart of events
  4. Identify contributing factors – patient, task, individual, team, environment, equipment, organisation and communication factors
  5. Find root causes using tools:
    • "Five whys" – repeatedly asking "why?" until the basic cause is found
    • Fishbone (Ishikawa / cause-and-effect) diagram – grouping causes under headings such as people, methods, materials, machines, environment and management
  6. Develop an action plan – strong actions (system changes, forcing functions, standardisation) rather than weak actions (reminders only)
  7. Implement, monitor and share learning

4. Example

  • Incident – a patient received another patient's insulin
  • Five whys – why? Wrong patient's insulin pen taken → why? Pens stored together unlabelled → why? No individual storage → why? Policy not updated → why? No system review after earlier near misses
  • Actions – individual labelled pens stored in patients' bins, barcode scanning of pens, staff training

5. Principles – focus on systems, not blame; confidentiality; evidence-based; timely

6. Strength of actions

  • Strong actions (most effective) – change the system so that the error becomes difficult: forcing functions (oral syringes that cannot connect to IV lines), removal of high-risk drugs from wards, barcode scanning, standardised equipment
  • Intermediate actions – checklists, double checks, reduced workload, software enhancements
  • Weak actions (least effective) – reminders, warnings, new policies, re-training alone
  • An RCA should aim for strong and intermediate actions, not only telling staff to "be more careful"

Conclusion Root cause analysis is a structured investigation of serious incidents that uses tools such as the five whys and fishbone diagram to find and correct underlying system causes, so that similar events are prevented.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is a sentinel event?
answer_html:
A sentinel event is an unexpected patient safety event resulting in death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm, not related to the natural course of the illness.

Examples – surgery on the wrong site or wrong patient, a retained instrument or swab after surgery, haemolytic transfusion reaction due to ABO incompatibility, infant abduction or discharge to the wrong family, a fall resulting in death, a serious medication error causing death.

Action – immediate care of the patient, reporting, root cause analysis and action to prevent recurrence. The word "sentinel" means the event signals the need for immediate investigation.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is a near miss? Why should it be reported?
answer_html:
Definition A near miss (close call) is an error or unsafe event that was caught before it reached the patient, or reached the patient without causing harm.

Example – a nurse notices before giving a drug that it is prescribed for another patient with a similar name.

Why report

  • Near misses show weak points in the system before harm occurs
  • They are more frequent than harmful events, so they give more learning opportunities
  • Reporting is free of blame and helps prevent future harm

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA)?
answer_html:
FMEA is a proactive (prospective) risk assessment method used to study a process step by step to find what could go wrong (failure modes), why (causes) and what the effects would be – before an error happens.

Steps – select a high-risk process (e.g. blood transfusion, chemotherapy), map the steps, identify failure modes, score each for severity, occurrence and detectability to get a risk priority number, then redesign the process for the highest-risk failures and monitor.

Difference from RCA – FMEA is done before an incident; RCA is done after.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is alert fatigue? How can it be prevented?
answer_html:
Alert fatigue is the state in which clinicians, exposed to too many alerts and alarms, become desensitised and begin to ignore or override them, including important ones.

Causes – excessive, irrelevant or repetitive computer alerts; frequent monitor alarms with false positives.

Prevention

  • Show only clinically important, specific alerts; grade them by severity (tiered alerts)
  • Regularly review and remove unhelpful alerts
  • Set individualised alarm limits on monitors; good electrode care
  • Train staff and involve users in alert design

Example – a nurse who hears constant false SpO₂ alarms may silence the monitor and miss a real fall in oxygen saturation.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: List the International Patient Safety Goals.
answer_html:
The International Patient Safety Goals (Joint Commission International), also reflected in accreditation standards such as NABH, are:

  1. Identify patients correctly – at least two identifiers
  2. Improve effective communication – read-back of verbal orders and critical results, structured handover
  3. Improve the safety of high-alert medications – including concentrated electrolytes
  4. Ensure safe surgery – correct site, correct procedure, correct patient (surgical safety checklist)
  5. Reduce the risk of health care–associated infections – hand hygiene
  6. Reduce the risk of patient harm resulting from falls

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain standardised nursing terminologies – NANDA-I, NIC, NOC and the Omaha System – and their importance in nursing informatics.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses all over the world often describe the same problem, intervention or outcome in different words. Computers cannot compare or analyse such varied language. Standardised nursing terminologies (SNTs) give nursing a common, structured language so that nursing care can be documented, shared, measured and researched in electronic records.

PART A – MEANING

  • A standardised nursing terminology is a set of defined terms (and codes) describing nursing diagnoses, interventions and outcomes, agreed upon by the profession and suitable for use in electronic systems

PART B – NANDA-I (nursing diagnoses)

  • Developed by NANDA International (originally North American Nursing Diagnosis Association, 1982)
  • Provides standard labels for nursing diagnoses, each with a definition, defining characteristics, related factors and risk factors
  • Organised in Taxonomy II with 13 domains and many classes (e.g. Domain 4 Activity/Rest, Domain 11 Safety/Protection)
  • Types – problem-focused, risk, health promotion and syndrome diagnoses
  • Example – Impaired gas exchange; Risk for falls

PART C – NIC (Nursing Interventions Classification)

  • Developed at the University of Iowa
  • A comprehensive list of nursing interventions (independent and collaborative), each with a label, definition and a list of activities
  • Arranged in domains and classes (e.g. physiological basic, physiological complex, behavioural, safety, family, health system, community)
  • Example – intervention "Fall prevention" with activities such as assessing risk, keeping the call bell within reach, using bed alarms

PART D – NOC (Nursing Outcomes Classification)

  • Also from the University of Iowa
  • Standard patient outcomes sensitive to nursing interventions, each with a definition, indicators and a 5-point measurement (Likert) scale (e.g. 1 = severely compromised to 5 = not compromised)
  • Domains include functional health, physiological health, psychosocial health, health knowledge and behaviour, perceived health, family health and community health
  • Example – outcome "Fall prevention behaviour" rated before and after teaching

PART E – NNN LINKAGE

  • NANDA-I, NIC and NOC are linked – for each diagnosis there are suggested outcomes and interventions
  • Example – Risk for falls (NANDA-I) → Fall prevention (NIC) → Falls occurrence / Fall prevention behaviour (NOC)
  • This linkage makes care planning in electronic systems quick and consistent

PART F – THE OMAHA SYSTEM

  • Developed by the Visiting Nurse Association of Omaha (USA) for community and home health nursing; now used in many settings
  • Three components:
    1. Problem Classification Scheme – 42 client problems in 4 domains: environmental, psychosocial, physiological and health-related behaviours
    2. Intervention Scheme – 4 categories: teaching, guidance and counselling; treatments and procedures; case management; surveillance, with targets and specific details
    3. Problem Rating Scale for Outcomes – rates knowledge, behaviour and status each on a 5-point scale, at intervals, to measure progress
  • Example – Problem: Medication regimen; Intervention: teaching about insulin; Outcome: knowledge rating improved from 2 to 4

PART G – OTHER TERMINOLOGIES

  • ICNP (International Classification for Nursing Practice) – developed by the International Council of Nurses for worldwide use
  • Clinical Care Classification (CCC), perioperative and other specialty data sets
  • Nursing concepts are also included in SNOMED CT and LOINC (e.g. nursing assessments)

PART H – IMPORTANCE IN NURSING INFORMATICS

  1. Common language – clear communication among nurses across settings and countries
  2. Electronic documentation – structured, coded entries for care plans in EHRs
  3. Visibility of nursing – shows nurses' contribution to patient outcomes
  4. Data for research and quality – comparison of outcomes, nursing-sensitive indicators
  5. Decision support – linking assessment data to suggested diagnoses and interventions
  6. Staffing and costing – measuring nursing workload
  7. Education – teaching structured clinical reasoning

Limitations – need for training, translation to local languages, time to document, and licensing costs for some terminologies

PART I – Example of an electronic care plan using NNN

  • Patient – a 50-year-old man on the first day after abdominal surgery
  • NANDA-I diagnosis – Acute pain related to the surgical incision, evidenced by pain score 7/10 and guarding
  • NOC outcome – Pain level, indicator "reported pain" rated 2 (substantial) at baseline, target 4 (mild) within 24 hours
  • NIC intervention – Pain management: assess pain every 4 hours, give prescribed analgesics, teach splinting and relaxation breathing, position for comfort
  • Evaluation – after 24 hours the rating is 4; the computer stores the coded data, which can later be analysed for all post-operative patients on the ward

Conclusion Standardised nursing terminologies – NANDA-I for diagnoses, NIC for interventions, NOC for outcomes, the Omaha System for community care, and ICNP – give nursing a common, coded language that makes care documentable, shareable and measurable in electronic systems and makes nursing's contribution visible.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define clinical decision support system (CDSS). Explain its components, types, examples, advantages, limitations and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Clinicians must make many decisions quickly with large amounts of information – it is easy to miss an allergy, an abnormal result or an interaction. Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) bring relevant knowledge and patient data together at the right time to help clinicians make better decisions.

A. Definition

  • A CDSS is a computer system that provides clinicians, patients and others with knowledge and patient-specific information, intelligently filtered and presented at appropriate times, to enhance health and health care
  • It supports, not replaces, clinical judgement

B. Purposes

  • Improve patient safety – prevent errors
  • Improve quality – evidence-based, consistent care
  • Improve efficiency – save time, reduce unnecessary tests
  • Support diagnosis and treatment planning

C. Components (knowledge-based CDSS)

  1. Knowledge base – rules ("IF the patient is allergic to penicillin AND amoxicillin is prescribed, THEN show an alert"), drug databases, guidelines
  2. Inference engine – combines the rules with the patient's data from the EHR to produce advice
  3. Communication mechanism (user interface) – displays alerts, reminders or suggestions in the clinician's workflow

D. Types

  • Knowledge-based – uses explicit rules and guidelines
  • Non-knowledge-based – uses machine learning / artificial intelligence to find patterns in data (e.g. predicting sepsis or readmission)
  • Active (interruptive) – pop-up alerts that require a response
  • Passive – information available when the user looks (e.g. info buttons, reference links)

E. Forms of decision support

  • Alerts – allergy, drug–drug interaction, duplicate therapy, dose-range checks, critical lab values
  • Reminders – vaccinations, screening tests, repositioning a patient, catheter removal review
  • Order sets and care pathways – standard groups of orders for common conditions
  • Documentation templates with built-in prompts
  • Calculators – drug doses by weight, IV drip rates, risk scores (BMI, Braden, GCS)
  • Early warning scores – automatic NEWS2 or sepsis screening from vital signs
  • Diagnostic support – lists of possible diagnoses; image analysis (AI)
  • Reference information – drug monographs, guidelines

F. Examples in nursing

  • Fall-risk and pressure-injury risk scores calculated automatically, with suggested interventions
  • Sepsis alert when temperature, pulse and respiratory rate cross set limits
  • Insulin dosing protocols based on blood glucose
  • Reminders to reassess pain after an analgesic or to turn a patient two-hourly
  • Care plan suggestions linked to nursing diagnoses (NANDA-I – NIC – NOC)

G. Advantages

  • Fewer medication errors and adverse events
  • Earlier detection of deterioration
  • Evidence-based, standardised care; better adherence to guidelines
  • Saves time; supports less experienced staff; continuous learning

H. Limitations

  • Alert fatigue – too many alerts are ignored
  • Over-reliance (automation bias); loss of critical thinking
  • Outdated or incorrect rules; poor integration with workflow
  • Bias in AI systems trained on limited data; lack of transparency
  • Cost, maintenance and legal questions about responsibility

I. Role of the nurse

  • Enter accurate data – decision support is only as good as the data
  • Respond thoughtfully to alerts and document reasons for overriding
  • Use clinical judgement – check that advice fits the patient
  • Report inappropriate or excessive alerts; help design nursing decision support
  • Keep up to date with guidelines built into the system

J. Example of decision support in action

  • A patient's vital signs entered by the nurse – temperature 38.8 °C, pulse 118/min, respiratory rate 26/min, BP 92/60 mmHg – produce a high early warning score
  • The system shows a sepsis alert, suggests the sepsis order set (blood cultures, lactate, IV fluids, antibiotics) and notifies the doctor and rapid response team
  • The nurse confirms the findings at the bedside, informs the doctor, starts the protocol as ordered and increases observation frequency

K. The "five rights" of clinical decision support

  • The right information (evidence-based and relevant)
  • To the right person (doctor, nurse, pharmacist or patient)
  • In the right format (alert, order set, reminder, graph)
  • Through the right channel (EHR, mobile device, portal)
  • At the right time in the workflow (when the decision is being made)
  • Following these "rights" makes decision support useful and reduces alert fatigue

L. Evaluating a CDSS

  • Check whether alerts are acted upon or overridden, whether errors and adverse events have decreased, and whether users find the system helpful; remove or improve alerts that are not useful

Conclusion A clinical decision support system combines a knowledge base, an inference engine and a user interface to deliver patient-specific alerts, reminders, order sets, calculators and early warnings; it improves safety and quality, but must be well designed and used with clinical judgement, accurate data and attention to alert fatigue.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain knowledge management in clinical and policy decisions.
answer_html:
Introduction Health organisations hold a huge amount of knowledge – in research papers, guidelines, records and in the experience of their staff. Knowledge management (KM) makes sure that this knowledge is captured, shared and used in daily clinical decisions and in health policy.

1. Definition

  • Knowledge management is the systematic process of creating, capturing, organising, sharing and applying knowledge to improve decisions and performance

2. Types of knowledge

  • Explicit knowledge – written, recorded and easy to share – guidelines, protocols, textbooks, research articles, databases
  • Tacit knowledge – personal knowledge from experience and skill – e.g. an experienced nurse's sense that a patient is deteriorating; harder to share

3. Processes of knowledge management

  1. Creation – research, audits, experience, innovation
  2. Capture and storage – documentation, databases, repositories, intranets
  3. Organisation – classification, indexing, standard terminologies
  4. Sharing – training, mentoring, case discussions, journal clubs, communities of practice, e-learning
  5. Application – using knowledge in decisions through protocols and decision support
  6. Review and updating

4. Use in clinical decisions

  • Clinical practice guidelines and standard operating procedures available at the point of care
  • Decision support in the EHR (alerts, order sets)
  • Access to evidence databases (Cochrane, PubMed) and drug references
  • Lessons learnt from incident analysis shared across wards

5. Use in policy decisions

  • Data from HMIS, surveillance and research guide decisions on programmes, budgets, staffing and new services
  • Evidence summaries and health technology assessment inform government policy

6. Tools – intranet portals, document management systems, e-learning platforms, discussion forums, dashboards

7. Nurse's role – share expertise, document lessons, participate in guideline development and use evidence in practice

8. Barriers and facilitators

  • Barriers – lack of time, heavy workload, poor access to computers or internet, information overload, a culture of not sharing, hierarchy, and outdated documents
  • Facilitators – supportive leadership, easy-to-use portals, regular journal clubs and case discussions, mentoring of new nurses by experienced staff, recognition of staff who share knowledge

9. Example – after a needle-stick injury review, the ward's learning is written into a short guideline, shared at a staff meeting and uploaded to the hospital intranet so that every ward can use it.

Conclusion Knowledge management captures, organises, shares and applies explicit and tacit knowledge, so that clinical and policy decisions are based on the best available evidence and experience.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain SNOMED CT and its mapping to ICD-10-CM.
answer_html:
Introduction Health records need two kinds of coding: detailed clinical terms for patient care (what exactly the clinician observed), and broader classification codes for statistics, billing and reporting. SNOMED CT serves the first purpose and ICD the second. Mapping links them, so that data recorded once can serve both purposes.

1. SNOMED CT

  • Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Clinical Terms, maintained by SNOMED International
  • The most comprehensive clinical terminology in the world, with hundreds of thousands of concepts – clinical findings, diseases, procedures, body structures, organisms, substances, observations
  • Each concept has a unique numeric code, descriptions (synonyms) and relationships (e.g. "pneumonia" is a "lung disease")
  • Used inside EHRs for detailed clinical documentation and decision support
  • India has a national release centre and has made SNOMED CT available free for use in the country

2. ICD-10-CM

  • International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification (a version of WHO's ICD-10 used in the USA); WHO's ICD-10 and the newer ICD-11 are used internationally
  • A classification that groups diseases into categories for statistics, morbidity and mortality reporting, insurance and billing

3. Mapping

  • Mapping is creating links from SNOMED CT concepts to the matching ICD codes
  • The clinician records the condition in detail with SNOMED CT; the system suggests or generates the ICD-10-CM code automatically using the map
  • Example – a detailed SNOMED CT concept for a specific type of pneumonia is mapped to the corresponding ICD-10-CM pneumonia category

4. Benefits of mapping

  • Record once, use many times – care, billing and statistics from the same entry
  • Reduces manual coding work and errors
  • Consistent national and international data
  • Supports research and public health reporting

5. Challenges

  • SNOMED CT is more detailed than ICD, so some maps are one-to-many or need extra information (e.g. age, laterality); some maps need human review
  • Maps need regular updating as both systems change

Conclusion SNOMED CT is a detailed clinical terminology for recording care, while ICD-10-CM is a classification for statistics and billing; mapping SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM lets data entered once in the EHR be used for both care and reporting.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is SNOMED CT?
answer_html:
SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Clinical Terms) is the most comprehensive multilingual clinical terminology in the world, maintained by SNOMED International.

  • Contains hundreds of thousands of concepts – findings, disorders, procedures, body structures, organisms, substances – each with a unique code, synonyms and relationships
  • Used in EHRs to record clinical information precisely, so that it can be shared, analysed and used for decision support
  • Supports semantic interoperability; India provides it free for national use

Example – the concept Myocardial infarction (disorder) has the SNOMED CT identifier 22298006.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is ICD-11?
answer_html:
ICD-11 is the 11th revision of the International Classification of Diseases, published by the World Health Organization, adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and in effect from 1 January 2022.

Features

  • Fully digital, designed for use in electronic records
  • Alphanumeric codes; around 17,000 categories with many more index terms
  • New chapters (e.g. traditional medicine, sexual health, conditions related to gaming)
  • Allows combining codes ("post-coordination") for detail

Uses – recording and reporting causes of death and illness, health statistics, insurance and planning.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is LOINC?
answer_html:
LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes) is a standard coding system for laboratory tests and clinical observations, developed by the Regenstrief Institute (USA) and available free.

  • Each test or observation has a unique code – e.g. separate codes for serum glucose, HbA1c, blood pressure, pain score
  • Ensures that a result from one laboratory is understood correctly by another system
  • Used with SNOMED CT (for findings) and HL7/FHIR (for exchange) to achieve semantic interoperability

Example – LOINC code 4548-4 identifies haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) measured in blood.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is a clinical practice guideline?
answer_html:
Definition A clinical practice guideline is a set of systematically developed recommendations, based on the best available evidence, to help clinicians and patients make decisions about appropriate care for specific conditions.

Examples – WHO guidelines, ICMR standard treatment workflows, national guidelines for TB (NTEP), hypertension and diabetes, infection-control guidelines.

Uses – standardise care, reduce variation, improve quality and safety; can be built into decision support systems in EHRs.

Note – guidelines support, but do not replace, clinical judgement and patient preferences.

Good guidelines are evidence-based, clear, regularly updated and developed by experts with input from users and patients.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define eHealth. Explain its components, benefits and challenges. Add a note on eHealth initiatives in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Information and communication technology (ICT) has changed how people learn about health, consult health workers and manage their own illness. Mobile phones and the internet now reach even remote villages. eHealth uses these technologies to make health services more accessible, efficient and patient-centred. India has many large digital health programmes that nurses use daily.

A. Definition

  • eHealth is the use of information and communication technologies (ICT) for health – for health services, health surveillance, health education, knowledge and research
  • The broader term digital health includes newer technologies such as mobile apps, wearables, artificial intelligence and big data

B. Components of eHealth

  1. Electronic health records and hospital information systems
  2. Telemedicine and telehealth – remote consultation, diagnosis, monitoring and teaching (telenursing, teleradiology, telepsychiatry)
  3. mHealth (mobile health) – health services and information through mobile phones, SMS, voice messages and apps
  4. Consumer health informatics – health websites, patient portals, personal health records, online communities
  5. Health information systems for programmes and public health (HMIS, surveillance)
  6. e-Learning for health workers
  7. e-Prescribing and online pharmacy services
  8. Wearable devices and remote monitoring – BP monitors, glucometers, fitness trackers linked to apps
  9. Health data analytics and AI

C. Benefits

  • Access – care reaches rural and remote people without travel
  • Saves time and cost for patients and health systems
  • Continuity of care – records available anywhere
  • Patient empowerment – people understand and manage their health
  • Better public health – faster surveillance, programme monitoring and outbreak response
  • Training of health workers at scale
  • Support during emergencies (e.g. teleconsultation during COVID-19)

D. Challenges

  • Digital divide – lack of smartphones, internet, digital literacy, especially among the poor, elderly and rural women
  • Language barriers and low health literacy
  • Misinformation on the internet and social media
  • Privacy and security of personal health data
  • Infrastructure – electricity, connectivity, devices
  • Interoperability of many separate apps and portals
  • Limits of remote care – no physical examination; need for clear guidelines and accountability
  • Resistance and workload for health workers who must enter data in many portals

E. eHealth initiatives in India

  • Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) – digital health ecosystem with ABHA health IDs, registries of professionals and facilities, consent-based record sharing
  • eSanjeevani – the national telemedicine service: doctor-to-doctor consultations from Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (health and wellness centres) with specialists at hubs, and patient-to-doctor OPD consultations from home
  • Tele-MANAS – national tele-mental health helpline (toll-free number 14416) launched in 2022
  • Nikshay – web and mobile platform for tuberculosis patient notification, treatment monitoring and direct benefit transfer
  • U-WIN – digital registry for routine immunisation of children and pregnant women (following CoWIN used for COVID-19 vaccination)
  • RCH portal and ANMOL (ANM Online) – tracking of mothers and children by ANMs
  • Kilkari – free weekly audio messages to pregnant women and mothers about pregnancy and child care
  • HMIS portal – monthly facility health data; IHIP – disease surveillance platform
  • Mera Aspataal – patient feedback system
  • NCD portal / app for screening of hypertension, diabetes and common cancers

F. Role of the nurse

  • Use digital platforms accurately for documentation and reporting
  • Teach patients to use apps, teleconsultation and personal health records
  • Guide patients to reliable information; correct myths
  • Provide telenursing follow-up and support
  • Protect privacy and obtain consent
  • Help bridge the digital divide – assist those who cannot use technology

G. Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, 2020 (key points)

  • Issued in March 2020 to enable registered medical practitioners to provide care through telemedicine
  • Modes – video, audio and text (chat, e-mail, messaging)
  • Types – first consultation and follow-up; patient-to-doctor and health worker-to-doctor consultations (a nurse or health worker may connect the patient with the doctor)
  • The practitioner must identify the patient, obtain consent, use professional judgement on whether teleconsultation is suitable, and maintain records
  • Medicines are grouped into lists that may be prescribed in different modes; certain drugs (e.g. narcotics) cannot be prescribed through telemedicine
  • Privacy and confidentiality must be protected as in physical consultations

H. eHealth in a patient's journey – example

  • A woman in a village receives Kilkari voice messages during pregnancy
  • The ANM registers her in the RCH portal, links her ABHA and records antenatal visits on a tablet
  • At the health and wellness centre the community health officer arranges an eSanjeevani teleconsultation with a specialist when her BP rises
  • Her baby's vaccinations are recorded in U-WIN, which sends reminders for the next dose
  • All records are available to the hospital when she delivers – an example of connected digital care

Conclusion eHealth is the use of ICT for health, including EHRs, telemedicine, mHealth, consumer health tools, health information systems and e-learning; it improves access, efficiency and empowerment but faces the digital divide, misinformation and privacy challenges, and India's ABDM, eSanjeevani, Tele-MANAS, Nikshay, U-WIN and other initiatives show its growing role, in which nurses are key users and teachers.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define public health informatics. Explain its functions and applications, and the role of nurses.
answer_html:
Introduction Public health focuses on the health of populations – preventing disease, controlling outbreaks and planning services. All of this depends on timely and accurate information about who is sick, where, and why. Public health informatics applies information science and technology to these tasks. In India, nurses, ANMs and community health officers are among the largest contributors and users of public health data.

A. Definition

  • Public health informatics is the systematic application of information and computer science and technology to public health practice, research and learning – for surveillance, prevention, health promotion and planning

B. Functions

  1. Disease surveillance – continuous collection, analysis and interpretation of data on diseases, with timely feedback for action
  2. Outbreak detection and response – early warning signals, line lists, mapping of cases
  3. Monitoring of programmes – immunisation, maternal and child health, TB, NCDs, nutrition
  4. Registries – birth and death registration, cancer registries, disease-specific registries
  5. Health planning and resource allocation – where to place staff, supplies and facilities
  6. Health promotion – mass messaging through SMS, voice calls, social media and websites
  7. Research and evaluation – studying risk factors and the impact of programmes
  8. Emergency and disaster management – tracking needs and resources

C. Applications in India

  • Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) using the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) – near real-time reporting of epidemic-prone diseases (dengue, malaria, cholera, measles) from health facilities and laboratories, with GIS maps
  • HMIS portal – monthly reports from every public health facility on services and outcomes
  • RCH portal and ANMOL app – name-based tracking of pregnant women and children for antenatal care, delivery, immunisation and postnatal care
  • U-WIN – electronic immunisation registry with vaccination certificates and reminders
  • Nikshay – TB notification, treatment adherence and nutrition support payments
  • NCD screening applications – population-based screening for hypertension, diabetes and cancers at health and wellness centres
  • Civil Registration System – births and deaths
  • Geographic information systems (GIS) – mapping cases, water sources, health facilities

D. Components

  • Data sources – facilities, laboratories, community health workers, surveys, registries
  • Standards – case definitions, coding (ICD), data formats
  • Information systems – portals, mobile apps, databases, dashboards
  • People and governance – trained staff, policies on data quality and privacy

E. Benefits

  • Earlier detection of outbreaks and quicker response
  • Better targeting of services to high-risk groups and areas
  • Accountability and monitoring of programme performance
  • Evidence-based policy and planning

F. Challenges

  • Data quality – incomplete, late or inaccurate entries
  • Many separate portals, duplication of work, lack of interoperability
  • Connectivity and device problems in rural areas; training needs
  • Privacy of personal data in large databases

G. Role of nurses (including ANMs and community health officers)

  • Collect and enter accurate data – registration of pregnant women, births, immunisations, TB cases, screening results – in registers and apps
  • Report notifiable diseases promptly and maintain line lists during outbreaks
  • Analyse local data – e.g. drop-out children for immunisation, high-risk pregnancies – and act on it (home visits, referrals)
  • Health education using mHealth tools; encourage use of Kilkari and other services
  • Use dashboards and monthly reports in meetings for planning
  • Maintain confidentiality of community members' data
  • Take part in surveillance during campaigns and disasters

H. Example – detecting a dengue outbreak

  • Health facilities in a district report fever and dengue test results daily on IHIP
  • The district surveillance unit sees a sharp rise in cases from one area on the dashboard map
  • A rapid response team investigates; ANMs and ASHAs carry out house-to-house fever surveys, larval source reduction and health education
  • Daily data show when cases decline, guiding when to scale down the response

I. Improving data quality – steps for health workers

  1. Use the correct case definitions and forms
  2. Record immediately after the service, not from memory later
  3. Check entries for completeness and errors before submitting
  4. Cross-check registers with portal entries every month
  5. Discuss data discrepancies in monthly meetings and correct them

  6. Use the data locally – data that are used are usually better maintained

  7. Protect confidentiality of every person's data, especially in sensitive programmes such as TB, HIV and mental health

Conclusion Public health informatics uses information technology for surveillance, outbreak response, programme monitoring, registries, planning and health promotion; in India IHIP, HMIS, the RCH portal, U-WIN, Nikshay and NCD systems are major applications, and nurses play a vital role in collecting accurate data and using it for action in the community.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define telenursing. Explain its applications, advantages and challenges.
answer_html:
Introduction Telenursing is the use of telecommunication technology to deliver nursing care and services at a distance. It became much more common during the COVID-19 pandemic and is now part of national telehealth services.

1. Definition

  • Telenursing is the delivery, management and coordination of nursing care and services using telecommunication technologies – telephone, video calls, mobile apps, remote monitoring devices and the internet

2. Applications

  • Follow-up after discharge – checking wounds, pain, medicines and warning signs
  • Chronic disease management – diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, COPD (remote BP, glucose and weight monitoring)
  • Telephone triage and advice lines – helping callers decide on the right level of care
  • Health education and counselling – breastfeeding, antenatal advice, lifestyle change
  • Home care and palliative care support; elderly care
  • Tele-mental health support (e.g. helplines)
  • Teleconsultation support – nurses at health and wellness centres assist patients during specialist teleconsultations (e.g. eSanjeevani)
  • Tele-education of nurses and nursing students

3. Advantages

  • Access for rural, elderly and disabled patients; saves travel time and cost
  • Continuity of care and early detection of problems; fewer readmissions
  • Patient satisfaction and empowerment
  • Efficient use of nursing staff; reduced exposure to infection

4. Challenges

  • No physical examination; risk of missing signs
  • Technology problems – connectivity, devices, power
  • Privacy and confidentiality – secure platforms needed
  • Legal issues – licensure, accountability, documentation, consent
  • Patients' digital literacy and language barriers

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Verify identity, obtain consent and ensure privacy
  • Follow protocols for triage and advice; know when to refer for in-person care
  • Document each contact accurately in the record
  • Use clear, simple language and check understanding

6. Example – telephone follow-up after discharge

  • The nurse calls the patient two days after a hernia operation, confirms identity and asks about pain, wound (redness, discharge), fever, bowel movements, diet and medicines
  • She reminds him of warning signs (bleeding, high fever, severe pain, vomiting) that need immediate care and confirms the date of the follow-up visit
  • She documents the call, the advice given and any referral in the patient's record

Conclusion Telenursing delivers nursing care at a distance through telephone, video and remote monitoring for follow-up, chronic disease management, triage, education and home care; it improves access and continuity but requires protocols, consent, privacy and careful documentation.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain how patients use the internet for health information and how nurses can help them evaluate it.
answer_html:
Introduction Many patients now search the internet, watch videos or ask on social media before or after visiting a health worker. This can empower them, but much online information is inaccurate, outdated or commercially biased. Nurses help patients find and judge reliable information.

1. How patients use the internet

  • Searching about symptoms, diseases, tests and medicines
  • Watching videos and reading blogs; joining online support groups
  • Using apps – fitness, diet, diabetes and pregnancy trackers, medication reminders
  • Booking appointments, viewing reports, teleconsultation
  • Buying medicines online

2. Benefits

  • Better understanding and participation in care
  • Emotional support from others with the same condition
  • Preparation of questions for the doctor or nurse

3. Risks

  • Misinformation and false "miracle cures"
  • Anxiety caused by reading about worst-case possibilities ("cyberchondria")
  • Self-medication and stopping prescribed treatment
  • Privacy risks when sharing personal data on apps and social media

4. Criteria for evaluating online health information

  • Source/authority – who wrote it? Prefer government health departments, WHO, professional bodies, hospitals and universities
  • Evidence – are claims supported by research and references?
  • Currency – is the date recent and the information updated?
  • Purpose – is it to inform, or to sell a product? Check for advertisements and conflicts of interest
  • Accuracy and balance – does it agree with other reliable sources? Does it mention risks as well as benefits?
  • Privacy – does the website or app explain how personal data are used?

5. Nurse's role

  • Ask patients what they have read and correct misunderstandings without dismissing them
  • Recommend reliable websites and apps in the patient's language
  • Teach the evaluation criteria and encourage discussion with health workers before acting on online advice
  • Assess health literacy and use simple language, pictures and teach-back
  • Model good practice – nurses themselves should share only reliable information on social media

6. Examples of reliable sources – the World Health Organization, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and national programme websites, ICMR, professional associations, hospital and university websites, and international public health agencies; information in Indian languages from official sources should be preferred for patients.

Conclusion Patients increasingly use the internet and apps for health information, which brings both empowerment and the risk of misinformation; nurses help them judge information by source, evidence, date, purpose and balance, and guide them to reliable resources.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain mHealth (mobile health) and its uses.
answer_html:
Introduction India has hundreds of millions of mobile phone users, including in rural areas. mHealth uses mobile devices to deliver health information and services, making it one of the most powerful eHealth tools.

1. Definition

  • mHealth is the use of mobile devices – mobile phones, smartphones, tablets, wearable sensors – for health services and information

2. Uses

  • Health education and behaviour change – SMS and voice messages (e.g. Kilkari for pregnant women and mothers), videos
  • Reminders – appointments, medication adherence (e.g. TB, HIV, diabetes), immunisation due dates
  • Data collection by health workers – ANMs and ASHAs record visits and services in apps (e.g. ANMOL, RCH and NCD apps)
  • Remote monitoring – connected BP monitors, glucometers, pulse oximeters and wearables send readings to health workers
  • Teleconsultation – video consultation on smartphones (e.g. eSanjeevani OPD)
  • Personal health records – ABHA app to store and share records
  • Emergency services – ambulance apps, helplines
  • Decision support for health workers – digital checklists and algorithms
  • Surveillance – reporting of cases from the field

3. Advantages

  • Wide reach and low cost; available anytime
  • Real-time data; better adherence and follow-up
  • Supports community health workers in remote areas

4. Limitations

  • Not everyone has a smartphone or data; low literacy; language issues
  • Battery, network and device problems
  • Privacy risks; too many apps; unverified apps of poor quality

5. Nurse's role – recommend reliable apps, teach their use, use official apps accurately for reporting, and protect patients' data

6. How to choose a health app

  • Developed or recommended by a government body, hospital, university or professional association
  • Based on evidence and updated regularly
  • Has a clear privacy policy; asks only for needed permissions
  • Available in the user's language, easy to use and free or affordable
  • Avoid apps that promise cures or sell products aggressively

7. Examples

  • Kilkari – weekly voice messages to pregnant women and mothers
  • Medication reminder SMS for TB and diabetes patients
  • ABHA app – storing and sharing health records
  • eSanjeevani OPD app – teleconsultation from home

Conclusion mHealth uses mobile devices for health education, reminders, data collection, remote monitoring, teleconsultation and personal records; it extends care to large populations at low cost, provided issues of access, literacy and privacy are addressed.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Differentiate between telemedicine and telehealth.
answer_html:
Telemedicine Telehealth
Use of telecommunication technology to provide clinical medical services at a distance – diagnosis, treatment, consultation Broader term – includes telemedicine plus non-clinical services
Mainly doctor–patient or doctor–doctor Includes nurses, pharmacists, educators, administrators
Examples – teleconsultation, teleradiology, telepathology Examples – telenursing, health education, training of health workers, administrative meetings, remote monitoring

In India, telemedicine is guided by the Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (2020).

Note – telenursing is a part of telehealth; both telemedicine and telehealth require patient consent, privacy, identification and documentation.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Differentiate between real-time and store-and-forward telemedicine.
answer_html:
• Real-time (synchronous) telemedicine – the patient and provider interact at the same time through video or audio calls; e.g. a live video consultation with a specialist
  • Store-and-forward (asynchronous) telemedicine – information such as photographs, X-rays, ECGs, reports or messages is collected and sent to a specialist, who reviews it later; e.g. teleradiology, teledermatology, tele-ophthalmology
  • Remote patient monitoring – a third mode, in which devices send health data (BP, glucose, weight) continuously or regularly to the care team

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is eSanjeevani?
answer_html:
eSanjeevani is the National Telemedicine Service of India, launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2019 and developed by C-DAC.

Two modes

  1. Doctor-to-doctor (hub-and-spoke) – patients at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (health and wellness centres) are connected, with the help of the community health officer or nurse, to doctors and specialists at hub hospitals
  2. Patient-to-doctor (eSanjeevani OPD) – citizens consult doctors from home through a mobile app or website

Benefits – free consultations, e-prescriptions, reduced travel, better access in rural areas; it is one of the largest government telemedicine services in the world.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is Tele-MANAS?
answer_html:
Tele-MANAS (Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) is India's national tele-mental health programme, launched in October 2022.

Features

  • Toll-free helpline 14416 (also 1-800-891-4416), available 24 × 7 in many languages
  • Callers receive counselling by trained counsellors, with referral to mental health professionals, teleconsultation or nearby services when needed
  • Linked with district mental health services and eSanjeevani

Nurse's role – inform patients and families about the service and encourage early help-seeking.

The service is free and confidential.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is Nikshay?
answer_html:
Nikshay is the web-based and mobile patient management system of India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP).

Uses

  • Notification of TB cases by public and private providers
  • Recording of diagnosis, treatment and follow-up for each patient
  • Monitoring treatment adherence
  • Direct benefit transfer of nutritional support (Nikshay Poshan Yojana) to patients' bank accounts
  • Programme reports and dashboards

Nurse's role – accurate registration and updating of patient records, adherence support and counselling.

It also supports contact tracing, reporting of drug side effects and monitoring towards the goal of a TB-free India.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the nursing information system (NIS) – its components (subsystems), functions, advantages and challenges.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses are the largest group of health professionals and the main users of patient information. A nursing information system (NIS) supports nurses in clinical care, management, education and research, and is usually a part of the hospital information system.

A. Definition

  • A nursing information system is a computer-based system that collects, stores, processes, retrieves, displays and communicates timely information needed for nursing practice, nursing administration, education and research

B. Components (subsystems)

1. Patient care (clinical) subsystem

  • Nursing assessment on admission and ongoing assessments
  • Vital signs charting, early warning scores, intake–output, pain scores
  • Nursing care plans using standardised terminologies (NANDA-I, NIC, NOC)
  • Nursing notes and progress records; handover (shift) reports
  • eMAR and barcode medication administration
  • Risk assessments – falls, pressure injuries, nutrition, VTE
  • Patient education records and discharge planning

2. Nursing management (administrative) subsystem

  • Staffing and scheduling – duty rosters, leave, overtime
  • Patient classification (acuity) and workload measurement to match staff to patients' needs
  • Personnel records – qualifications, registration, training, appraisal
  • Budgeting and cost control
  • Inventory of supplies and equipment
  • Quality monitoring – incident reports, audits, nursing-sensitive indicators
  • Bed management and census reports

3. Nursing education subsystem

  • Staff development records, in-service education schedules
  • Competency tracking and certification (e.g. BLS)
  • E-learning modules and assessments
  • Student clinical placement and evaluation records

4. Nursing research subsystem

  • Data warehouse of nursing data; tools for analysis
  • Access to literature databases and evidence-based protocols
  • Support for audits and quality-improvement projects

C. Functions

  • Collect patient and management data at the point of care
  • Process data into information (charts, trends, scores, reports)
  • Store data securely and retrieve it quickly
  • Communicate information to the health team
  • Support decisions – alerts, reminders, care plan suggestions
  • Generate reports for managers and authorities

D. Advantages

  • Legible, complete and timely nursing documentation
  • Saves time on charting and calculations; reduces duplication
  • Improved patient safety (eMAR, alerts, risk scores)
  • Continuity of care and better handovers
  • Evidence for staffing decisions through acuity data
  • Visibility of nursing work and outcomes; data for quality improvement and research
  • Better management of staff, supplies and budgets

E. Challenges

  • Cost of hardware, software and training
  • Resistance to change; time needed to learn
  • Poor design may increase documentation time and reduce patient contact
  • Downtime, technical faults
  • Privacy and security concerns
  • Lack of standardised nursing terminologies in some systems; poor integration with other modules

F. Requirements for a good NIS

  • User-friendly, designed with nurses' input to fit the nursing workflow
  • Uses standard terminologies and integrates with the HIS
  • Mobile access at the bedside; reliable and secure
  • Adequate training and support

G. Example of NIS use during a shift

  • At the start of the shift the nurse opens the electronic handover and sees her patients' summaries, pending orders and alerts
  • She records vital signs on a tablet; the system calculates the early warning score and flags one patient with a rising score
  • She gives medicines using barcode scanning; the eMAR records the times automatically
  • She updates the care plan and nursing notes, records intake–output and a fall-risk reassessment
  • The nurse manager views the acuity scores of all patients and moves a nurse from a less busy ward
  • At the end of the month the system produces reports on falls, pressure injuries and missed doses for the quality meeting

H. Steps in implementing an NIS

  1. Form a team with nurses, IT staff and managers; study the existing workflow
  2. Select or design the system with standard nursing terminologies
  3. Test the forms with nurses; train all staff and identify ward "super-users"
  4. Start in a pilot ward, correct problems, then expand
  5. Evaluate – documentation quality, time spent, safety indicators and user satisfaction

I. Role of the nurse

  • Use the system accurately and promptly; never share passwords
  • Give feedback on problems and suggest improvements
  • Use the information (alerts, trends, reports) to improve patient care

  • Maintain confidentiality and follow downtime procedures

  • Help new staff and students learn to use the system safely

Conclusion A nursing information system supports patient care, nursing management, education and research through subsystems for documentation, care planning, medication administration, staffing, acuity, quality monitoring, staff development and data analysis, improving safety, efficiency and the visibility of nursing when it is well designed and properly supported.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the evaluation, analysis and presentation of health care data to inform management decisions.
answer_html:
Introduction Managers in health care – nurse managers, hospital administrators and programme officers – must decide on staffing, budgets, equipment, services and quality improvement. Good decisions require data that are collected properly, analysed correctly and presented clearly. Without this, decisions are based on guesswork.

PART A – SOURCES OF DATA

  • Hospital information system – admissions, discharges, bed occupancy, length of stay, deaths
  • Registers and records – nursing records, medication charts, incident reports
  • Audits – documentation, hand hygiene, infection control
  • Surveys – patient satisfaction, staff satisfaction
  • Financial and stores data – costs, consumption
  • National and state portals – HMIS reports for public facilities

PART B – EVALUATION OF DATA (CHECKING QUALITY)

  • Is the data accurate, complete, timely, consistent and valid?
  • Are definitions the same across wards and months (e.g. what counts as a "fall")?
  • Are there missing values or obvious errors (e.g. impossible ages)?
  • Is the sample large enough to draw conclusions?

PART C – INDICATORS USED IN MANAGEMENT

1. Hospital indicators

  • Bed occupancy rate, average length of stay, bed turnover rate, mortality rates, infection rates, readmission rates

2. Nursing-sensitive indicators

  • Patient falls and falls with injury
  • Hospital-acquired pressure injuries
  • Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) and central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)
  • Medication errors
  • Nurse–patient ratio, nursing hours per patient day, staff turnover and absenteeism
  • Patient satisfaction with nursing care

3. Types of indicators (Donabedian)

  • Structure – resources (staff numbers, equipment)
  • Process – how care is given (percentage of patients assessed for fall risk)
  • Outcome – results (fall rate per 1,000 patient days)

PART D – ANALYSIS OF DATA

  • Descriptive statistics – counts, percentages, rates (e.g. falls per 1,000 patient days), means and medians
  • Trends over time – comparing month to month; run charts and control charts show whether changes are real or due to chance
  • Comparison with targets and benchmarks (other wards, hospitals, national standards)
