  • Pareto analysis – identifying the few causes responsible for most problems (80/20 rule)
  • Cost analysis – cost per patient day, cost of supplies
  • Root causes – combining data with incident analysis

PART E – PRESENTATION OF DATA

  • Tables – exact figures, clearly titled
  • Bar charts – comparison between wards or categories
  • Line graphs and run charts – trends over time
  • Pie charts – proportions (use for few categories)
  • Histograms – distribution of continuous data (e.g. length of stay)
  • Dashboards and scorecards – key indicators on one screen with colour codes (green, amber, red)
  • Maps (GIS) – geographical distribution
  • Principles – simple, accurate, clearly labelled (title, axes, units, source, period), suited to the audience

PART F – USING THE INFORMATION FOR DECISIONS

  • Staffing – acuity and workload data guide the number and skill mix of nurses per shift
  • Budgeting and procurement – consumption data guide orders
  • Quality improvement – rising infection rates lead to bundle audits and training
  • Planning new services – demand data (e.g. dialysis waiting lists)
  • Policy and accreditation – evidence for NABH or national quality standards

PART G – EXAMPLE

  • Monthly dashboard shows pressure injury rate in a medical ward rising from 1.2 to 3.5 per 1,000 patient days
  • Analysis shows most cases in bedridden elderly patients on night shifts with low staffing
  • Decision – provide pressure-relieving mattresses, a two-hourly turning chart with electronic reminders and an extra night nurse; re-measure after three months
  • The rate falls to 1.0 – the decision was evaluated with data

PART H – Common errors in interpreting data

  • Comparing numbers instead of rates (a larger ward will have more falls; compare falls per 1,000 patient days)
  • Reacting to a single month's change that may be due to chance (use run charts over time)
  • Using different definitions in different wards or months
  • Ignoring missing data or reporting errors
  • Misleading graphs – unequal scales, cut-off axes, too many categories

PART I – Role of the nurse manager

  • Ensure accurate data collection by staff
  • Review indicators regularly with the team; display them on ward notice boards or dashboards
  • Use data to plan improvements and to justify resources

  • Share results with staff and celebrate improvements

  • Protect the confidentiality of patient and staff data in reports

Conclusion Health care data from information systems, records, audits and surveys must be checked for quality, analysed with rates, trends, benchmarks and tools such as run charts and Pareto analysis, and presented clearly in tables, graphs and dashboards so that managers can make and evaluate decisions on staffing, budgets, quality and services.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the common hospital statistics used in management, with formulas.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospital statistics are numerical measures of how a hospital's resources are used and what results are achieved. Nurse managers use them to plan beds, staff and services and to compare performance.

1. Bed occupancy rate (BOR)

  • BOR (%) = (Total inpatient days in a period × 100) ÷ (Number of beds × number of days in the period)
  • Example – 30-bed ward, 30 days, 810 inpatient days: (810 × 100) ÷ (30 × 30) = 90%
  • Very high occupancy (above about 85–90%) suggests overcrowding and strain on staff; low occupancy suggests under-use

2. Average length of stay (ALOS)

  • ALOS = Total inpatient days of discharged patients ÷ Number of discharges (including deaths)
  • Example – 810 days ÷ 162 discharges = 5 days
  • Long stays may indicate complications, delays in tests or discharge planning problems

3. Bed turnover rate

  • Bed turnover rate = Number of discharges (including deaths) ÷ Average number of beds
  • Example – 162 ÷ 30 = 5.4 patients per bed in the month

4. Turnover interval

  • Turnover interval = (Available bed days − Occupied bed days) ÷ Number of discharges
  • The average time a bed stays empty between patients; example – (900 − 810) ÷ 162 ≈ 0.6 day

5. Death rates

  • Gross death rate (%) = (Total deaths × 100) ÷ Total discharges (including deaths)
  • Net death rate (%) = deaths excluding those within 48 hours of admission × 100 ÷ (discharges − deaths within 48 hours) – reflects the quality of care more fairly

6. Other indicators

  • Hospital-acquired infection rate per 1,000 patient days or device days
  • Nurse–patient ratio; nursing hours per patient day
  • Readmission rate within 30 days

Nurse's role – keep accurate census and records (admissions, discharges, deaths, transfers), as all statistics depend on them; use the figures for staffing and quality decisions

7. Uses in planning – examples

  • A consistently high bed occupancy with long waiting lists supports a request for more beds or staff
  • A rising average length of stay in surgical wards leads to review of discharge planning and delays in investigations
  • A high turnover rate with short stays shows heavy nursing workload from frequent admissions and discharges

Conclusion Bed occupancy rate, average length of stay, bed turnover rate, turnover interval and death rates, calculated from accurate ward records, help nurse managers plan resources and evaluate the efficiency and quality of care.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the use of information systems in nurse staffing and scheduling.
answer_html:
Introduction Having the right number of nurses with the right skills at the right time is essential for patient safety. Manual rostering is time-consuming and often unfair. Staffing and scheduling systems use patient and staff data to plan nursing workforce more accurately.

1. Patient classification (acuity) systems

  • Patients are classified by the amount of nursing care they need – e.g. self-care, minimal, intermediate, intensive (or numerical scores)
  • The system calculates the nursing hours required per shift from these scores
  • Helps match staff to actual workload rather than to the number of beds alone

2. Workload measurement – time studies, nursing activity scores, number of procedures, admissions and discharges per shift

3. Scheduling (rostering) software

  • Prepares duty rosters automatically according to rules (shift patterns, rest days, skill mix, legal limits on hours)
  • Manages leave requests, shift swaps and overtime
  • Sends rosters and changes to staff mobile phones
  • Tracks attendance (biometric systems)

4. Advantages

  • Safer staffing matched to patient needs; fewer understaffed shifts
  • Fair and transparent rosters; better staff satisfaction
  • Saves managers' time
  • Data for decisions – justification for new posts, budget planning, identifying overtime and absenteeism
  • Links with quality indicators (e.g. falls versus staffing levels)

5. Limitations

  • Acuity tools must be valid and used consistently
  • Software cost and training needs
  • Cannot replace the manager's judgement about staff competence and sudden changes

6. Role of the nurse manager

  • Ensure accurate acuity scoring every shift; use reports to adjust staffing; review rosters for fairness and skill mix; protect staff data

7. Example of an acuity-based calculation

  • A 30-bed ward has 10 patients needing minimal care (about 2 nursing hours/day), 15 intermediate (about 4 hours) and 5 intensive (about 8 hours)
  • Required nursing hours = (10 × 2) + (15 × 4) + (5 × 8) = 120 hours per day
  • With 8-hour shifts this equals 15 nurse-shifts per day, distributed between morning, evening and night, plus extra staff for leave (relief)
  • The software repeats this calculation every shift as patients' scores change

Conclusion Information systems support nurse staffing through patient acuity classification, workload measurement and automated scheduling, giving safer, fairer and more efficient rosters and data for management decisions.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the methods of presenting health care data.
answer_html:
Introduction After data are collected and analysed, they must be presented clearly so that readers – managers, colleagues, students or the community – can understand them quickly and correctly.

1. Tabular presentation

  • Tables arrange data in rows and columns
  • Should have a number, clear title, column and row headings, units, totals and the source
  • Used to show exact figures (e.g. monthly admissions by ward)

2. Graphical (diagrammatic) presentation

  • Bar diagram – bars of equal width with length proportional to the value; for comparing categories (e.g. infections in different wards); simple, multiple or component bars
  • Histogram – adjacent bars showing the frequency distribution of continuous data (e.g. age groups, length of stay)
  • Frequency polygon – a line joining the midpoints of histogram bars
  • Line graph – shows trends over time (e.g. monthly fall rate); run charts add a median line
  • Pie chart – a circle divided into sectors showing proportions of a whole (e.g. causes of admission); best for few categories
  • Scatter diagram – shows the relationship between two variables (e.g. staffing level and falls)
  • Pictogram – pictures representing quantities, useful for community audiences
  • Maps – spot maps and GIS maps showing geographical distribution of cases

3. Dashboards

  • A single screen summarising key indicators with numbers, small charts and colour codes (green – on target, amber – warning, red – action needed); updated regularly from the information system

4. Principles of good presentation

  • Simple, accurate and honest – no misleading scales
  • Clear labels – title, axes, units, legend, period and source
  • Choose the right type of chart for the data
  • Avoid clutter and too many colours; suit the audience

5. Choosing the right method

  • Comparison between groups – bar diagram
  • Trend over time – line graph or run chart
  • Parts of a whole – pie chart
  • Distribution of a measurement – histogram
  • Relationship between two measurements – scatter diagram
  • Exact values – table
  • Where cases occur – map

Example – a nurse manager presents monthly fall rates on a line graph, causes of falls on a Pareto bar chart, and the current month's figures in a table on the ward dashboard.

Conclusion Health care data are presented as tables, bar diagrams, histograms, line graphs, pie charts, scatter diagrams, pictograms, maps and dashboards; choosing the right method and following principles of clarity and accuracy help managers and others understand and act on the data.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is a dashboard in health care management?
answer_html:
A dashboard is a visual display of the most important information (key indicators) on a single screen, updated regularly or in real time from information systems, so that managers can monitor performance at a glance.

Features – numbers, small charts and colour codes (green, amber, red) showing whether targets are met; ability to "drill down" into details.

Examples in nursing – bed occupancy, patients waiting for admission, fall rate, pressure injury rate, CAUTI rate, medication errors, staffing levels per shift, patient satisfaction scores.

Use – quick decisions, early detection of problems, comparison between wards and over time.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is a key performance indicator (KPI)?
answer_html:
A key performance indicator is a measurable value that shows how well an organisation, department or person is achieving important objectives.

Characteristics – specific, measurable, linked to goals, with a target and a time period (often called SMART).

Examples in nursing

  • Fall rate per 1,000 patient days
  • Percentage of patients with pain reassessed within 1 hour of analgesia
  • Hand hygiene compliance rate
  • Bed occupancy rate, average length of stay
  • Staff turnover rate

KPIs are displayed on dashboards and compared with targets and benchmarks to guide action.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What are nursing-sensitive indicators?
answer_html:
Nursing-sensitive indicators are measures of the structure, process and outcomes of care that are directly affected by the quantity and quality of nursing care.

Examples

  • Structure – nurse–patient ratio, nursing hours per patient day, percentage of qualified nurses
  • Process – pain assessment, fall-risk and pressure-injury risk assessment completed on admission
  • Outcome – patient falls, hospital-acquired pressure injuries, CAUTI, CLABSI, medication errors, patient satisfaction with nursing care

Use – monitoring and improving the quality of nursing care, and showing nursing's contribution to patient outcomes.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is a Pareto chart?
answer_html:
A Pareto chart is a bar chart in which causes or categories of a problem are arranged in descending order of frequency, with a line showing the cumulative percentage.

Principle – the Pareto (80/20) principle: about 80% of problems come from about 20% of causes.

Example – analysis of medication errors shows that wrong time and omitted doses make up most errors, so improvement efforts are focused on these first.

Use – helps managers prioritise the "vital few" causes in quality improvement.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: Explain the ethical and legal issues related to health care information in clinical practice, with reference to Indian laws.
answer_html:
Introduction Health information is among the most sensitive personal information a person has – it can reveal illnesses such as HIV, mental illness, pregnancy or genetic conditions. Its misuse can cause stigma, discrimination, financial loss and emotional harm. With electronic records, information can be copied and shared in seconds, so nurses must understand the ethical principles and laws that govern its use. Information governance is the framework of policies and practices that ensures information is handled legally, securely, ethically and efficiently.

PART A – ETHICAL PRINCIPLES APPLIED TO HEALTH INFORMATION

  • Autonomy – patients have the right to decide who sees their information; informed consent for sharing
  • Beneficence – information is used to benefit the patient (continuity of care, safety)
  • Non-maleficence – avoid harm from disclosure, loss or misuse of data
  • Justice – fair access to information and to digital services; no discrimination
  • Fidelity – keeping the trust placed in health professionals
  • Veracity – honest and accurate records; no falsification

PART B – MAJOR ETHICAL AND LEGAL ISSUES

1. Confidentiality and privacy

  • Privacy – the patient's right to control personal information; confidentiality – the professional's duty not to disclose it without permission
  • Information is shared only with those directly involved in care ("need to know")

2. Consent

  • Consent is needed for sharing records with other providers, family, insurers or researchers (except where law requires disclosure)
  • Consent-based sharing is the basis of ABDM's health information exchange

3. Access and ownership

  • The physical/electronic record is maintained by the hospital, but the information belongs to the patient, who has a right to access and obtain copies of his records as per rules
  • Unauthorised access ("snooping" into records of celebrities, colleagues or relatives) is a serious breach

4. Accuracy and integrity of records

  • Records must be complete, accurate and timely; never alter, back-date or destroy records; corrections are made openly (with audit trail)
  • Falsifying records is unethical and illegal and may amount to misconduct or a criminal offence

5. Retention and disposal

  • Records must be kept for the period required by law and policy (e.g. at least 3 years for indoor patients under medical council regulations, longer for medico-legal cases and minors); disposed of securely (shredding, secure deletion)

6. Disclosure without consent (exceptions)

  • Court orders and police requests in medico-legal cases
  • Notifiable diseases to public health authorities
  • Mandatory reporting – e.g. sexual offences against children under the POCSO Act
  • Serious risk of harm to the patient or others

7. Use of data for research and secondary purposes

  • Requires ethics committee approval, informed consent or anonymisation/de-identification

PART C – INDIAN LAWS AND GUIDELINES

  • Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended 2008) – gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures; provides penalties for hacking, data theft and other cyber offences
  • Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 – personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose with consent (or certain legitimate uses); principles of purpose limitation and data minimisation; rights of the person to access, correction, erasure and grievance redressal; duties of organisations (data fiduciaries) to protect data and report breaches; a Data Protection Board; heavy penalties
  • HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 – protects the confidentiality of HIV status; disclosure only with consent or as allowed by the Act
  • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 – right to confidentiality of mental health information
  • Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act – confidentiality of the woman's identity
  • POCSO Act, 2012 – mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse
  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019 – patients may seek compensation for deficient services, where records are key evidence
  • Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 and state rules – maintenance of records
  • Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, 2020 – privacy, consent and records in teleconsultation
  • ABDM Health Data Management Policy – rules for consent, sharing and protection of health data in the digital health ecosystem
  • Indian Nursing Council Code of Ethics – nurses must respect privacy and confidentiality

PART D – NURSE'S RESPONSIBILITIES

  • Access only the records needed for one's duties; use one's own login; log out
  • Share information only with authorised persons; check identity before giving information on the telephone
  • Never discuss patients in public places or post on social media
  • Obtain consent before sharing, photographing or recording patients
  • Keep records accurate and honest; follow retention and disposal policies
  • Report breaches and suspicious activity immediately
  • Know the exceptions where disclosure is legally required and follow hospital procedure

Conclusion Health information must be handled according to ethical principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, fidelity and veracity; the main issues are confidentiality, consent, access, integrity, retention, permitted disclosure and secondary use, governed in India by the IT Act, the DPDP Act, the HIV and Mental Healthcare Acts, POCSO and other laws and guidelines, and nurses protect patients by accessing, sharing and recording information responsibly.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: Explain the security of health information – threats, safeguards and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospitals have become frequent targets of cyber-attacks because health records are valuable and hospitals depend on computers for every service. In November 2022, a ransomware attack on AIIMS New Delhi disrupted its computer systems for many days, showing how attacks can affect patient care. Information security protects health data and systems from such threats.

PART A – GOALS OF INFORMATION SECURITY (CIA TRIAD)

  1. Confidentiality – information is available only to authorised persons
  2. Integrity – information is accurate and not altered without authorisation
  3. Availability – information and systems are accessible when needed for care

PART B – THREATS

  • Hacking and unauthorised access from outside
  • Ransomware – malicious software that locks or encrypts data and demands payment
  • Phishing – fake e-mails or messages that trick staff into revealing passwords or clicking harmful links
  • Malware and viruses from pen drives, downloads and attachments
  • Insider threats – staff viewing records without need, sharing passwords, selling data
  • Lost or stolen devices – laptops, phones, pen drives containing patient data
  • Social engineering – tricking staff by telephone or in person
  • Sharing patient information on personal messaging apps and social media
  • System failures, power cuts, fire and floods – loss of availability

PART C – SAFEGUARDS

1. Administrative safeguards

  • Information security policies and an information governance committee
  • Role-based access – each user sees only what the job requires
  • Training and awareness programmes on phishing, passwords and privacy
  • Regular audits of access logs; disciplinary action for breaches
  • Incident response plan – reporting cyber incidents to the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) within the time required and following its directions
  • Contracts with vendors requiring data protection

2. Physical safeguards

  • Locked server rooms, controlled entry, CCTV
  • Computer screens placed away from public view; privacy filters
  • Secure storage of devices; secure disposal of old computers and paper records (shredding)

3. Technical safeguards

  • Unique user IDs and strong passwords; two-factor authentication for remote and sensitive access
  • Automatic log-off after inactivity
  • Encryption of data stored and transmitted
  • Firewalls, antivirus and anti-malware software; regular updates and patches
  • Audit trails – automatic records of who accessed or changed what and when
  • Regular backups, stored separately (offline or off-site), and tested disaster recovery plans
  • Network segmentation – separating medical devices and clinical systems from general networks

PART D – NURSE'S RESPONSIBILITIES

  • Never share passwords or log in for others; create strong passwords and change them regularly
  • Lock or log out of the computer when leaving it, even briefly
  • Do not open suspicious e-mails, links or attachments; report them to the IT department
  • Do not store patient data on personal phones, pen drives or personal e-mail; avoid sharing patient details or photos through personal messaging apps
  • Keep screens and printouts out of public view; collect printouts immediately; shred confidential paper
  • Report lost devices, suspected breaches or unusual system behaviour immediately
  • Follow downtime procedures during outages
  • Access records only on a need-to-know basis

PART E – Example: responding to a ransomware attack

  1. Screens show a message that files are locked and payment is demanded
  2. Staff stop using the affected computers, do not click further and inform the IT department and management at once
  3. Infected systems are disconnected from the network to stop spread
  4. Wards switch to downtime procedures – paper charts, printed medication lists, telephone communication
  5. The incident is reported to CERT-In and other authorities as required; experts investigate
  6. Systems are restored from clean backups; passwords are changed; data entered on paper are entered back later
  7. A review identifies weaknesses (e.g. outdated software, phishing e-mail) and training and controls are strengthened

PART F – Creating strong passwords

  • Use long passphrases (12 or more characters) mixing words, numbers and symbols; avoid names, birthdays and "123456"
  • Use a different password for each important system; never write it on the computer or share it
  • Change it if there is any suspicion that it is known to others

PART G – Use of personal mobile devices

  • Use only hospital-approved apps for clinical communication
  • Protect phones with a screen lock; do not store patient photos or data in personal galleries or chats
  • Report a lost phone that had access to hospital systems immediately

Conclusion Security of health information aims at confidentiality, integrity and availability, and protects against hacking, ransomware, phishing, insider misuse, device loss and system failures through administrative, physical and technical safeguards such as role-based access, training, audits, encryption, two-factor authentication, audit trails and backups; every nurse shares the responsibility by protecting passwords, logging out, avoiding unsafe sharing and reporting incidents promptly.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: Explain the ethical and legal issues of digital health in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Digital health – telehealth, mobile apps, EHRs, artificial intelligence and social media – brings new ethical and legal questions for nurses in addition to the traditional duties of confidentiality and good care.

1. Consent and patient choice

  • Patients must understand and agree to teleconsultation, data sharing and use of apps; they may refuse and choose in-person care
  • Consent for photographs, video recording and remote monitoring

2. Privacy and security

  • Use only approved, secure platforms for patient communication; avoid sending patient details through personal messaging apps
  • Protect data collected by apps and wearable devices

3. Accountability and standard of care

  • The same standard of care applies online as in person; the nurse is accountable for advice given remotely
  • Work within the scope of practice and licensure; follow telehealth protocols; know when to refer for physical examination

4. Documentation integrity

  • Accurate electronic records; avoid copy-and-paste errors; never use another person's login
  • Electronic records are legal documents and are admissible as evidence under the IT Act

5. Equity and the digital divide

  • Elderly, poor, rural and less-literate people may be excluded from digital services; nurses must ensure alternatives and help them use services

6. Artificial intelligence and automation

  • AI tools may contain bias, make errors or lack transparency; the nurse must use professional judgement and not blindly follow computer advice
  • Responsibility for decisions remains with professionals

7. Professional boundaries and social media

  • Avoid "friending" patients, posting patient information or images, or giving individual advice publicly

8. Commercial and secondary use of data

  • Patient data must not be used for marketing or sold; research use requires approval and consent or anonymisation

Nurse's role – stay informed of policies and laws, use approved tools, obtain consent, document carefully, protect privacy and advocate for equitable access

Example – a nurse photographs a patient's wound and sends it to a doctor on a personal messaging app; this risks a privacy breach. The correct practice is to obtain the patient's consent and use the hospital's secure, approved system, recording the image in the patient's record.

Conclusion Digital health raises issues of consent, privacy, accountability, licensure, documentation integrity, equity, AI bias, social media conduct and secondary use of data; nurses meet these responsibilities by applying the same ethical standards online as in face-to-face care.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: Define confidentiality. Explain its principles, exceptions and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Confidentiality is one of the oldest principles of health care. Patients share personal details because they trust that health workers will keep them private. Breaking this trust harms the patient and the profession.

1. Definition

  • Confidentiality is the duty of health professionals to protect personal information shared by patients and not to disclose it without their consent, except where the law or patient safety requires it

2. Principles

  • Share information only on a need-to-know basis with those directly involved in care
  • Obtain consent before disclosing information to others (family, employers, insurers)
  • Disclose the minimum necessary information
  • Keep records secure (paper and electronic)
  • Respect special protection for sensitive information – HIV status, mental illness, pregnancy termination, sexual health, genetic information

3. Exceptions (disclosure without consent)

  • Legal requirement – court orders, police in medico-legal cases, notification of births and deaths
  • Public health – notifiable diseases to health authorities
  • Mandatory reporting – child sexual abuse (POCSO)
  • Serious risk to the patient or others (e.g. danger to a third person), as per law and policy
  • Sharing within the care team for treatment
  • Use of anonymised data for audit and research with approval

4. Nurse's responsibilities

  • Do not discuss patients in lifts, canteens, buses or on social media
  • Confirm identity before giving information by phone; give information to relatives only with the patient's permission
  • Protect records – log out, keep files closed, keep screens hidden from visitors
  • Ensure privacy during care (screens, curtains) and while taking histories
  • Report breaches and follow the hospital's confidentiality policy
  • Confidentiality continues after the patient's death and after the nurse leaves the job

5. Examples of breaches of confidentiality

  • Discussing a patient's diagnosis with neighbours or relatives without permission
  • Leaving case files open at the nurses' station where visitors can read them
  • Telling a caller about a patient's condition without confirming who the caller is
  • Looking up the record of a famous patient or a colleague out of curiosity
  • Posting a "funny" story about a patient on social media, even without the name

Conclusion Confidentiality is the professional duty to protect patients' personal information, shared only on a need-to-know basis with consent, except for legally defined situations; nurses protect it in conversation, records, telephone communication and digital media.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: Explain the guidelines for the professional use of social media by nurses.
answer_html:
Introduction Social media – WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, X and others – can be used by nurses for learning, networking and health promotion. However, careless use can breach patient confidentiality, damage the nurse's reputation and lead to disciplinary or legal action.

1. Benefits

  • Professional networking, sharing of evidence and educational resources
  • Health promotion campaigns for the public
  • Support groups and communication among professionals

2. Risks

  • Posting patient information, photographs or videos – even without names, patients may be identified
  • Unprofessional comments about patients, colleagues or employers
  • Blurring of professional boundaries with patients
  • Spreading misinformation
  • Permanent digital footprint; screenshots shared widely

3. Guidelines

  1. Never post patient information or images, even "anonymous" ones, without formal consent and institutional permission
  2. Do not discuss workplace incidents or criticise colleagues publicly
  3. Maintain professional boundaries – avoid personal relationships with patients on social media
  4. Separate personal and professional accounts; use privacy settings
  5. Do not give individual medical advice publicly; direct people to proper services
  6. Share only reliable, evidence-based health information; cite sources
  7. Do not use hospital logos or speak on behalf of the employer without permission
  8. Use only approved secure platforms for work communication about patients
  9. Think before posting – would it be acceptable to the patient, the employer and the nursing council?
  10. Report breaches you notice to the appropriate person

4. Consequences of misuse – disciplinary action by the employer, action by the nursing council, legal action under privacy and IT laws, loss of public trust

5. Positive professional uses

  • Sharing public health messages from official sources (e.g. vaccination drives, World Hand Hygiene Day)
  • Joining professional groups for learning and networking
  • Promoting nursing as a profession and celebrating achievements without patient details

6. Case example

  • A nurse posts a selfie in the ward; a patient's name and monitor display are visible in the background – this is a breach of confidentiality, even if unintended
  • Correct action – remove the post immediately, inform the supervisor, and in future take no photographs in clinical areas

Conclusion Social media offers nurses opportunities for learning and health promotion, but nurses must protect patient privacy, maintain professional boundaries, share reliable information and follow institutional and professional guidelines.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: What is an audit trail?
answer_html:
An audit trail is an automatic, time-stamped record kept by an information system of who accessed or changed what information, when and from where.

Uses

  • Detecting unauthorised access to patient records
  • Showing all changes to a record (original entry preserved) – important for legal cases
  • Investigating incidents and breaches
  • Encouraging responsible use of records

Note – because every access is recorded, nurses should open only the records needed for their work.

Audit trails cannot be altered by ordinary users and are reviewed regularly by the hospital.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: What is encryption?
answer_html:
Encryption is the process of converting readable data (plain text) into a coded form (cipher text) using a mathematical key, so that it cannot be read by unauthorised persons. Only those with the correct key can decrypt and read it.

Uses in health care

  • Protecting data stored on servers, laptops, phones and pen drives
  • Protecting data transmitted over networks (secure websites use https, secure messaging and telemedicine platforms)

Benefit – even if a device is lost or data are intercepted, the information remains protected.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: State the main features of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
answer_html:
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is India's law for the protection of digital personal data.

Main features

  1. Personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose, with the person's consent (or for certain legitimate uses defined in the Act)
  2. Notice must explain what data are collected and why; consent can be withdrawn
  3. Rights of the data principal – access to information, correction and erasure, grievance redressal, nominating another person
  4. Duties of data fiduciaries (organisations, including hospitals) – accuracy, security safeguards, reporting of breaches, deletion when no longer needed
  5. Special care for children's data
  6. A Data Protection Board of India to enforce the law, with heavy financial penalties for violations

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
unit_title: Information Law and Governance in Clinical Practice
question: What is the CIA triad in information security?
answer_html:
The CIA triad describes the three main goals of information security:

  1. Confidentiality – only authorised persons can access the information (e.g. passwords, role-based access, encryption)
  2. Integrity – information is accurate, complete and not altered without authorisation (e.g. audit trails, validation checks)
  3. Availability – information and systems are accessible when needed for patient care (e.g. backups, power backup, protection from ransomware)

All three are essential – for example, a ransomware attack mainly destroys availability, while unauthorised viewing breaks confidentiality.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define evidence-based practice. Explain its components, steps, levels of evidence, the role of informatics, barriers and facilitators.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing practices were once based largely on tradition, habit and authority ("we have always done it this way"). Research has shown that some traditional practices are ineffective or even harmful. Evidence-based practice (EBP) ensures that nursing care is based on the best current evidence, combined with clinical expertise and the patient's preferences, giving better outcomes and safer, more cost-effective care.

PART A – DEFINITION

  • Evidence-based practice is the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of the best available research evidence, integrated with clinical expertise and patient values and preferences, in making decisions about the care of individual patients

PART B – COMPONENTS

  1. Best research evidence – from well-designed studies and systematic reviews
  2. Clinical expertise – the nurse's skills, experience and judgement
  3. Patient values and preferences – beliefs, culture, choices
  4. Clinical context and resources – the setting, available staff, equipment and cost

PART C – STEPS OF EBP

  1. Cultivate a spirit of inquiry – questioning current practices
  2. Ask a clinical question in PICO format – Patient/population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (sometimes Time)
    • Example: "In adult ICU patients (P), does oral care with chlorhexidine (I) compared with saline (C) reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia (O)?"
  3. Acquire the best evidence – search databases (Cochrane Library, PubMed, CINAHL), guidelines and evidence summaries
  4. Appraise the evidence critically – validity, reliability, applicability, level of evidence
  5. Apply – integrate the evidence with clinical expertise and patient preferences to change practice (protocols, training)
  6. Assess (evaluate) the outcome – audit results after implementation
  7. Disseminate – share results with colleagues, conferences, publications

PART D – LEVELS (HIERARCHY) OF EVIDENCE (one common scheme)

  • Level I – systematic reviews or meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials (RCTs); evidence-based clinical practice guidelines
  • Level II – at least one well-designed RCT
  • Level III – controlled trials without randomisation
  • Level IV – case-control and cohort studies
  • Level V – systematic reviews of descriptive and qualitative studies
  • Level VI – a single descriptive or qualitative study
  • Level VII – opinion of authorities and expert committees
  • Higher levels are generally stronger, but the best evidence depends on the type of question (e.g. qualitative studies for patients' experiences)

PART E – ROLE OF INFORMATICS IN EBP

  • Electronic databases and digital libraries for rapid literature search
  • Reference management software
  • Clinical decision support – evidence-based alerts, order sets and care pathways built into the EHR
  • Point-of-care tools – mobile access to guidelines and drug information at the bedside
  • E-learning and webinars for teaching EBP
  • Data from EHRs – to measure outcomes before and after practice changes and to generate new evidence
  • Statistical software for analysing data

PART F – BARRIERS TO EBP

  • Lack of time and heavy workload
  • Limited skills in searching and appraising research; limited English proficiency
  • Poor access to databases, journals and computers
  • Resistance to change and organisational culture; lack of support from managers
  • Lack of authority to change practice; few nurse researchers or mentors
  • Research findings not relevant to local settings

PART G – FACILITATORS

  • Supportive leadership and protected time for EBP
  • Training in research and EBP; journal clubs
  • Access to databases and the internet; librarian support
  • EBP mentors and nurse researchers; collaboration with nursing colleges
  • Incentives and recognition; inclusion of EBP in policies and accreditation

PART H – EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE-BASED NURSING PRACTICES

  • Kangaroo mother care and immediate skin-to-skin contact for newborns
  • Early initiation of breastfeeding within one hour
  • Care bundles for preventing catheter, central line and ventilator infections
  • Hand hygiene using alcohol-based hand rub
  • Two-hourly repositioning and pressure-redistributing mattresses for pressure injury prevention
  • Early mobilisation after surgery

PART I – ROLE OF THE NURSE

  • Question routine practices; formulate PICO questions
  • Search and appraise evidence; take part in journal clubs and EBP projects
  • Implement and evaluate evidence-based protocols; involve patients in decisions

PART J – Example of EBP in a ward

  • Nurses notice that many patients develop phlebitis from IV cannulas
  • PICO question: in adult medical patients, does re-siting cannulas when clinically indicated with regular site checks, compared with routine re-siting, affect phlebitis and infection?
  • They search the evidence, appraise guidelines and systematic reviews, introduce a phlebitis scoring tool and regular site checks, and audit results after three months
  • Phlebitis falls and unnecessary cannulations are reduced – the results are shared at a hospital meeting

Conclusion Evidence-based practice integrates the best research evidence with clinical expertise, patient preferences and context, through the steps of asking, acquiring, appraising, applying, assessing and disseminating; evidence is graded from systematic reviews down to expert opinion, informatics greatly supports every step, and supportive leadership, training and access help nurses overcome barriers.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define quality of health care. Explain its dimensions, approaches to quality improvement and quality assurance programmes in India. Add a note on the role of informatics.
answer_html:
Introduction Patients expect care that is safe, effective and respectful. Quality of health care has become a central concern of hospitals and governments, supported by accreditation, national quality standards and information systems. Nurses, as the largest workforce, are key to quality.

PART A – DEFINITION

  • Quality of care is the degree to which health services for individuals and populations increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge
  • In simple words – doing the right thing, the right way, at the right time, for the right person, with the best possible results

PART B – DIMENSIONS OF QUALITY (WHO)

  1. Effective – based on evidence and producing the desired results
  2. Safe – minimising harm to patients
  3. People-centred – respecting individual preferences, needs and values
  4. Timely – reducing waiting times and harmful delays
  5. Equitable – no variation in quality because of sex, caste, religion, location or income
  6. Integrated – coordinated across levels and providers
  7. Efficient – maximum benefit from available resources, avoiding waste - (The Institute of Medicine lists six aims – safe, timely, effective, efficient, equitable and patient-centred – STEEEP)

PART C – APPROACHES TO QUALITY IMPROVEMENT

1. Donabedian model

  • Structure (resources – staff, equipment, buildings) → Process (how care is given) → Outcome (results – recovery, complications, satisfaction)

2. PDSA (Plan–Do–Study–Act) cycle

  • Small, rapid tests of change: plan a change, try it, study the results, act (adopt, adapt or abandon)

3. Total quality management (TQM) and continuous quality improvement (CQI)

  • Involves everyone in the organisation in constantly improving processes, with focus on the customer (patient)

4. Six Sigma – a data-driven method to reduce variation and defects (DMAIC: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control)

5. Lean – removing waste (waiting, unnecessary movement, duplication) to make processes smoother

6. Clinical audit, benchmarking, standard operating procedures, checklists, care bundles and accreditation

PART D – QUALITY ASSURANCE PROGRAMMES IN INDIA

  • NABH (National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers) – a constituent board of the Quality Council of India (set up in 2006); accredits hospitals and other health organisations; also offers Nursing Excellence certification
  • NQAS (National Quality Assurance Standards) – for public health facilities (district hospitals, CHCs, PHCs, health and wellness centres), under the National Health Mission
  • Kayakalp – awards public health facilities for cleanliness, hygiene and infection control (since 2015)
  • LaQshya – improving quality of care in labour rooms and maternity operation theatres (since 2017)
  • MusQan – quality of child-friendly services in public facilities (since 2021)
  • International accreditation – e.g. JCI for some hospitals; NABL for laboratories

PART E – ROLE OF INFORMATICS IN QUALITY

  • Quality indicators collected automatically from the HIS – infection rates, falls, readmissions, waiting times
  • Dashboards and run charts for monitoring
  • Clinical decision support – evidence-based order sets and alerts
  • Electronic incident reporting and risk registers
  • Registries and patient feedback systems (e.g. Mera Aspataal)
  • Audit tools and electronic checklists

PART F – ROLE OF THE NURSE

  • Follow standards, protocols and SOPs; participate in audits and quality circles
  • Collect accurate quality data and use it to improve care
  • Report incidents; implement care bundles; take part in PDSA projects
  • Ensure patient-centred, respectful care and patient education
  • Prepare the ward for accreditation (documentation, infection control, patient rights)

PART G – Patient rights and patient experience

  • The Charter of Patients' Rights (Government of India) and accreditation standards emphasise information, informed consent, privacy, dignity, non-discrimination, second opinion and grievance redressal
  • Patient feedback and satisfaction surveys are important quality measures; complaints are investigated and used for improvement

PART H – Examples of nursing quality indicators

  • Patient falls and pressure injuries per 1,000 patient days
  • CAUTI and CLABSI rates; hand hygiene compliance
  • Medication errors and near misses reported
  • Pain reassessment after analgesia; completeness of nursing documentation
  • Patient satisfaction with nursing care; nurse–patient ratio and staff turnover

PART I – Cost of poor quality

  • Poor quality leads to complications, longer stays, readmissions, legal claims and loss of public trust; improving quality therefore also saves money and protects the hospital's reputation

Conclusion Quality of health care is the degree to which services achieve desired outcomes in line with current knowledge; it is effective, safe, people-centred, timely, equitable, integrated and efficient, is improved through Donabedian's model, PDSA, TQM, Six Sigma, Lean and audit, and is assured in India through NABH, NQAS, Kayakalp, LaQshya and MusQan, with informatics providing the data and tools and nurses providing much of the improvement.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the technical and professional informatics standards.
answer_html:
Introduction Standards are agreed rules or specifications that make health information systems safe, compatible and of good quality. In informatics there are technical standards (for systems and data) and professional standards (for the people who use and manage them).

A. Technical standards

  1. Data exchange standards – HL7 version 2, CDA and FHIR for clinical messages and documents; DICOM for medical images
  2. Terminology and classification standards – SNOMED CT (clinical terms), LOINC (laboratory tests and observations), ICD-10/ICD-11 (diseases), nursing terminologies (NANDA-I, NIC, NOC, ICNP)
  3. Medical device communication – IEEE 11073 standards for connecting devices such as monitors and pumps to information systems
  4. Record architecture – ISO 13606, openEHR
  5. Security and privacy – ISO standards for information security management, encryption and authentication standards
  6. Integration profiles – IHE (Integrating the Healthcare Enterprise) guidance on combining standards
  7. Standards bodies – ISO Technical Committee 215 (Health Informatics), HL7 International, SNOMED International, WHO
  8. National – India's EHR Standards (2016) and the technical standards and health data policies of the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission

B. Professional standards

  1. Scope and standards of nursing informatics practice – published by professional bodies (e.g. the American Nurses Association) describing the role and responsibilities of informatics nurses
  2. Informatics competencies for all nurses – basic computer skills, information literacy and information management (e.g. the TIGER initiative's competencies)
  3. Certification in nursing informatics in some countries
  4. Codes of ethics – confidentiality, privacy and integrity of records (e.g. Indian Nursing Council Code of Ethics)
  5. Education standards – informatics in nursing curricula (as in the INC B.Sc Nursing syllabus)
  6. Documentation standards – institutional and accreditation requirements for complete, accurate records

C. Importance

  • Interoperability and safe exchange of data
  • Quality and safety of systems and documentation
  • Competent workforce able to use technology effectively and ethically

Why nurses should know standards – nurses record most of the patient data that systems exchange, so their correct use of standard terms and structured fields directly affects interoperability and patient safety.

Conclusion Technical informatics standards (HL7, FHIR, DICOM, SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD, IEEE 11073, ISO 13606 and security standards) make systems interoperable and safe, while professional standards (scope and standards of practice, competencies, certification, ethics and education) ensure that nurses use information technology competently and responsibly.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Explain the PDSA cycle with an example.
answer_html:
Introduction The PDSA (Plan–Do–Study–Act) cycle, based on the work of Shewhart and Deming, is a simple model for testing changes on a small scale before applying them widely. It is widely used in quality improvement in hospitals.

1. Steps

  • Plan – identify the problem, set an aim (specific and measurable), decide what change to test, predict the result and plan how to collect data
  • Do – carry out the change on a small scale (one ward, one shift, a few patients); record what happens and any problems
  • Study – analyse the data; compare results with predictions; learn what worked and what did not
  • Act – adopt the change if successful, adapt it and test again, or abandon it; then plan the next cycle
  • Repeated cycles lead to continuous improvement

2. Example – reducing delays in giving antibiotics

  • Plan – audit shows only 40% of patients with suspected sepsis receive antibiotics within one hour; aim to reach 80% in three months; change: a sepsis alert and kit kept in the ward
  • Do – test the kit and alert in one medical ward for two weeks
  • Study – the rate rises to 70%; delays now occur at night because of pharmacy access
  • Act – adapt: keep first doses of common antibiotics in the ward emergency stock; test again – the rate reaches 85%; adopt and spread to other wards

3. Advantages

  • Low risk – changes are tested on a small scale
  • Encourages learning and staff involvement
  • Data-driven and quick

4. Role of informatics – electronic data for measuring baseline and progress; run charts and dashboards to display results

5. Tips for successful PDSA cycles

  • Start small (one ward, a few patients) and expand when the change works
  • Set a clear, measurable aim with a time frame
  • Involve the staff who do the work and the patients affected
  • Collect simple data often and display it on a run chart
  • Expect to run several cycles; learning from a "failed" test is still useful

Conclusion The PDSA cycle – plan, do, study, act – is a practical method of testing improvements on a small scale and refining them through repeated cycles, as in reducing delays in sepsis treatment.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Define clinical audit. Explain the audit cycle with an example.
answer_html:
Introduction Clinical audit is a quality improvement process that checks whether care meets agreed standards and, if not, improves it. It is one of the most practical tools for nurses to improve care.

1. Definition

  • Clinical audit is a systematic review of care against explicit criteria (standards), followed by implementation of change and re-audit, to improve patient care and outcomes

2. The audit cycle

  1. Select the topic – a high-risk, high-volume or problem area (e.g. pain reassessment, hand hygiene, documentation)
  2. Set standards (criteria) and targets – based on evidence or guidelines (e.g. "100% of patients given analgesia are reassessed within 1 hour")
  3. Collect data – from records, observation or electronic reports, using a checklist
  4. Compare the results with the standard
  5. Implement change – training, reminders, revised forms, system changes
  6. Re-audit – measure again to see whether practice has improved; continue the cycle

3. Example – documentation of pain reassessment

  • Standard – 100% of post-operative patients reassessed for pain within one hour of an analgesic
  • First audit – 30 records reviewed: 45% reassessed
  • Changes – a reminder in the electronic chart one hour after analgesic administration, staff teaching, pain scale displayed at each bed
  • Re-audit after two months – 88% reassessed; further changes planned for night shifts

4. Types

  • Standards-based audit (most common), adverse event review, peer review, patient surveys

5. Benefits

  • Improves care and outcomes; identifies training needs; supports accreditation; encourages teamwork

6. Role of informatics – electronic records make data collection faster; reports and dashboards show results; reminders support change

7. Clinical audit and research – the difference

  • Research creates new knowledge about what is the best practice; audit checks whether we are doing what we know is best
  • Research may involve new treatments and randomisation; audit measures current practice against standards without changing treatment for the purpose of the study
  • Research results are generalised widely; audit results apply mainly to the local setting
  • Research usually needs ethics committee approval; audit follows the hospital's quality procedures

Conclusion Clinical audit is a cycle of selecting a topic, setting standards, collecting data, comparing with standards, implementing change and re-auditing; it helps nurses improve care such as pain reassessment, with informatics making data collection and feedback easier.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: What is the PICO format?
answer_html:
PICO is a format for writing a focused clinical question in evidence-based practice:

  • P – Patient, population or problem (e.g. elderly post-operative patients)
  • I – Intervention (e.g. early mobilisation)
  • C – Comparison (e.g. routine bed rest)
  • O – Outcome (e.g. reduction in pneumonia)
  • (Sometimes T – Time frame is added – PICOT)

Example – "In elderly post-operative patients, does early mobilisation compared with routine bed rest reduce post-operative pneumonia?"

Use – identifies keywords for literature search and makes the question answerable.

subject: Health/Nursing Informatics and Technology
question: Differentiate between systematic review and meta-analysis.
answer_html:
• Systematic review – a review of all relevant studies on a clearly defined question, using systematic, explicit methods to search, select, appraise and summarise the evidence, reducing bias (e.g. Cochrane reviews)
  • Meta-analysis – a statistical technique that combines the numerical results of several similar studies (often within a systematic review) to produce a single pooled estimate of effect, with greater precision

Relationship – every meta-analysis should be based on a systematic review, but not every systematic review includes a meta-analysis (when studies are too different to combine).

Both are at the top of the hierarchy of evidence.

question: Explain Donabedian's model of quality.
answer_html:
Avedis Donabedian proposed that quality of care can be assessed through three linked components:

  1. Structure – the resources and setting of care: buildings, equipment, number and qualification of staff, policies (e.g. nurse–patient ratio)
  2. Process – what is done in giving and receiving care: assessments, procedures, communication (e.g. percentage of patients assessed for fall risk on admission)
  3. Outcome – the results of care for patients: recovery, complications, mortality, satisfaction (e.g. fall rate)

Principle – good structure increases the chance of good process, and good process increases the chance of good outcomes.

question: What is NABH?
answer_html:
NABH (National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers) is a constituent board of the Quality Council of India, set up in 2006, that accredits hospitals and other health care organisations in India.

Functions

  • Sets standards for patient safety and quality of care (patient rights, infection control, medication management, staffing, continuous quality improvement)
  • Assesses organisations and grants accreditation for a fixed period
  • Offers programmes such as Nursing Excellence certification, entry-level certification for small hospitals, and accreditation of blood banks and other services

Benefits – better quality and safety, patient confidence, recognition by insurers and government schemes.
